oneLine: HB 1055 opens Washington's Public Safety Employees' Retirement System (PSERS) Plan 2 to public safety telecommunicators (911 dispatchers) and their direct supervisors employed by PERS-covered public agencies, giving existing PERS 2/3 telecommunicators a one-time 2024 election to switch and requiring PSERS membership for new hires, while expressly excluding contract, nonprofit, and first-class city employees from coverage.

provisions.detail: Uncodified intent section limits the act's reach to newly-hired telecommunicators who would otherwise land in PERS 2/3, and to existing telecommunicators currently in PERS 2/3, while expressly disclaiming any intent to extend retirement membership to contract employees, nonprofit employees, or first-class city employees.
Amends the PSERS statement of legislative intent to add 'psychological' risk alongside physical risk as a basis for the plan's coverage rationale.

Expands the RCW 41.37.010 definition of 'employer' with a new catch-all category (12)(a)(xiii) covering any PERS chapter 41.40 employer some or all of whose employees primarily receive, process, transmit, or dispatch 911 emergency/nonemergency calls, if not already listed elsewhere in the employer definition.

Expands the RCW 41.37.010 definition of 'member' to add new subsection (19)(f) covering employees whose primary responsibility is 911 dispatch/call-processing (or supervision of such employees), making them PSERS-eligible.

Creates a one-time election window (January 1, 2024 through March 1, 2024) letting existing PERS 2/3 telecommunicators elect to become PSERS Plan 2 members as dual members under chapter 41.54 RCW; PERS service credit does not transfer to PSERS, and the new PSERS membership runs prospectively from the election date.
provisions.cites: new section to chapter 41.37 RCW; ch. 41.54 RCW

provisions.detail: Employees who do not affirmatively elect to move to PSERS by September 1, 2024 default to remaining in their current PERS plan.

Employees who were PERS Plan 1 members on or before June 1, 2019 and later become eligible telecommunicators must remain in PERS Plan 1 and are barred from moving to PSERS, creating a closed, permanently excluded subclass.
All employees newly hired on or after June 1, 2024 who meet the telecommunicator eligibility criteria are mandatorily enrolled in PSERS Plan 2 rather than PERS.
Sets a single effective date of June 1, 2024 for the entire act.

whoAffected: Public safety telecommunicators (911 dispatchers) and their direct supervisors employed by PERS-covered public agencies gain PSERS Plan 2 eligibility; contract, nonprofit, and first-class city dispatch employees, and pre-2019 PERS Plan 1 members, are excluded or locked out.
pointsOfInterest: The bill carves out contract employees, nonprofit employees, and first-class city employees from coverage even though they may perform identical dispatch work, making eligibility turn on employer type rather than job function.

The one-time election window (Jan-Mar 2024) with no PERS service-credit transfer to PSERS creates a self-selection dynamic: employees must weigh giving up PERS-side service credit continuity for PSERS benefit design, which could produce uneven uptake among otherwise similarly situated telecommunicators.

The PERS Plan 1 grandfather clause permanently locks a small, closed class of pre-June-2019 Plan 1 members out of PSERS even though they meet the new job-based eligibility test, splitting an otherwise identical job classification across two different plans indefinitely.

The new catch-all 'employer' definition (41.37.010(12)(a)(xiii)) sweeps in any PERS chapter 41.40 employer with qualifying dispatch employees, a broad residual category unlike the chapter's usual practice of naming specific state agencies, and could pull in numerous small cities, counties, and special districts not otherwise contemplated.

oneLine: SHB 1056 strikes the rule that barred PERS/SERS/TRS 2 and 3 members who retired under the 2008 'alternate early retirement' reduced-benefit schedule from the standard 867-hour postretirement employment allowance until age 65, and separately recalculates the benefit reduction (upward) for members who instead chose the 3%-per-year reduction option, effective January 1, 2024.

provisions.detail: Strikes the provision making a member who retired under the 2008 alternate early retirement schedule (30 service years, age 55+, age-based reduction table) ineligible for the 867-hour postretirement employment allowance until age 65, opening that allowance to them immediately upon retirement.

For members who chose the 3%-per-year alternate early retirement reduction rather than the 2008 formula (and its now-removed work restriction), directs recalculation of their benefit reduction to the more generous 2008 age-based schedule for payments made on or after the effective date, so they are not penalized relative to those who chose the restricted option.

Makes conforming strikes and renumbers subsections in the companion postretirement-reemployment sections that had cross-referenced the now-removed age-65 restriction on retirees under the alternate early retirement provisions, in TRS 2/3 and SERS 2/3.
Sets a specified future effective date rather than an immediate or emergency effective date.

whoAffected: PERS 2/3, SERS 2/3, and TRS 2/3 members who retired (or will retire) under the 2008 alternate early retirement formula (30 years service, age 55+), plus a smaller subgroup who instead chose the 3%-per-year reduction and now get a prospective benefit-reduction recalculation
pointsOfInterest: The affected class is defined entirely by a member's historical election among early-retirement options tied to the 2007-08 gain-sharing repeal litigation (chapter 41.31A RCW); the bill is unreadable without that background, a marker of narrow, path-dependent eligibility drafting.

Section 1's recalculation clause is a rare instance of the legislature adjusting a past member's benefit reduction upward to correct for an earlier choice made without full information (members who picked the 3% option to avoid work restrictions now being removed anyway), rather than a going-forward policy change.

The bill is purely conforming/deregulatory in substance (removes a return-to-work restriction) but touches nine RCW sections symmetrically across three systems and two plans each, so its length reflects structural repetition, not policy complexity.

No fiscal mechanics (no rate change, no new appropriation, no contingency) accompany a benefit-reduction recalculation that increases some members' allowances, suggesting SCPP/OSA scored the population and cost as immaterial.

oneLine: ESHB 1057 gives PERS 1 and TRS 1 retirees on the rolls as of July 1, 2022 a one-time 3 percent benefit increase (capped at $110/month) effective July 1, 2023, exempts the cost from the supplemental contribution rate, defers its inclusion in the standard employer UAAL rate until July 1, 2027, and directs SCPP to study an ongoing COLA.

provisions.detail: Adds subsection (4) granting TRS 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2022 a 3 percent increase to their monthly benefit, effective July 1, 2023, capped at $110.00.
Adds subsection (4) granting PERS 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2022 a 3 percent increase to their monthly benefit, effective July 1, 2023, capped at $110.00.
Renumbers the exclusion clause (new subsection (5)) so the TRS increase continues to not apply to beneficiaries receiving benefits under the separate minimum-benefit provisions.
Renumbers the exclusion clause (new subsection (5)) so the PERS increase continues to not apply to beneficiaries receiving benefits under the separate minimum-benefit provision.

Adds a proviso to the plan 1 UAAL benefit-improvement amortization language in the PERS, PSERS, and TRS employer contribution rate formulas providing that the rate for post-2009 benefit improvements shall not include a rate for this act's increase until July 1, 2027.
Adds new subsection (10) exempting the benefit increases granted to TRS 1 and PERS 1 members under this act from the supplemental contribution rate otherwise charged to fund benefit improvements.

New uncodified section directs the Select Committee on Pension Policy, during the 2023-2025 biennium, to study and recommend an ongoing COLA for PERS 1 and TRS 1 beneficiaries, coordinated with employer rate stability and reduction of the plan 1 unfunded liability.

Legislative findings section states the increase is a one-time measure addressing inflation-driven purchasing-power loss and that an ongoing COLA may not be affordable until UAAL contribution rates are reduced or eliminated.

whoAffected: PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 retirees/beneficiaries who were receiving a monthly benefit as of July 1, 2022, excluding those on the separate statutory minimum-benefit provisions (RCW 41.32.489, 41.32.540, 41.40.1984); cost borne by PERS/SERS/PSERS and TRS employers via deferred UAAL rate impact rather than a supplemental rate.
pointsOfInterest: The increase is walled off from the normal cost-recognition mechanics twice over: exempted entirely from the supplemental rate (Sec. 6) and excluded from the standard plan 1 UAAL benefit-improvement rate until July 1, 2027 (Sec. 5), a multi-year deferral of the fiscal footprint onto future rate-setting cycles.

Section 2 functions as a placeholder: it commits only to a one-time bump now while tasking SCPP with designing an ongoing COLA later, conditioned on employer rate stability and payoff of the plan 1 unfunded liability, signaling the legislature was unwilling to commit to recurring cost in this bill.

Continues the bill series' recurring eligibility-snapshot design (prior cohorts keyed to 2017, 2019, 2021 status dates now joined by a 2022 date), which by construction excludes anyone who retired or died between the snapshot date and the effective date, a hard eligibility cliff rather than a rolling COLA.

The carve-out excluding recipients of the RCW 41.32.489/.540 and 41.40.1984 minimum-benefit provisions means the lowest-benefit retiree subpopulation, already on a statutory floor, is the one group left out of this increase.

oneLine: HB 1201 amends RCW 41.45.060 and 41.45.150 to put fixed sunset dates on the existing minimum employer contribution rates that amortize the PERS 1 and TRS 1 unfunded liability, and layers on new four-year 0% supersession windows (TRS starting Sept. 2024, PERS/PSERS/SERS starting mid-2025, all running through 2029), converting an open-ended "until 100% funded" contribution floor into a scheduled, time-limited one.
whoAffected: Public employers in PERS, SERS, PSERS, and TRS (state agencies, local governments, school districts, and by extension PERS 1/TRS 1 retirees whose plans depend on continued UAAL funding)

provisions.detail: Amends RCW 41.45.060(6)(b), (7)(b), and (8)(b) to replace "subject to any minimum or maximum rates applied pursuant to" with "unless superseded by" RCW 41.45.150, conforming the PERS/PSERS and TRS employer UAAL-amortization formula to the new 0% supersession provisions added to .150.

Strikes "or maximum" from the "minimum or maximum rates" reference in RCW 41.45.060(6)(c), (7)(c), and (8)(c), removing the maximum-rate qualifier that had bounded benefit-improvement amortization surcharges collected in addition to RCW 41.45.150 rates.

Amends RCW 41.45.150(4) to add a fixed sunset of June 30, 2025 to the 3.50% minimum PERS/PSERS employer contribution for PERS 1 UAAL amortization, striking the prior open-ended condition that it remain effective "until the actuarial value of assets... equals one hundred percent of the actuarial accrued liability."
Amends RCW 41.45.150(5) to add a fixed sunset of August 31, 2025 to the 3.50% minimum SERS employer contribution for PERS 1 UAAL amortization, striking the same open-ended 100%-funded condition.
Amends RCW 41.45.150(6) to add a fixed sunset of August 31, 2024 to the 5.75% minimum TRS employer contribution for TRS 1 UAAL amortization, striking the same open-ended 100%-funded condition.
Adds new RCW 41.45.150(7) establishing a 0% contribution rate that supersedes the PERS/PSERS employer UAAL-amortization rate from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2029.
Adds new RCW 41.45.150(8) establishing a 0% contribution rate that supersedes the SERS employer UAAL-amortization rate from September 1, 2025 through August 31, 2029.

Adds new RCW 41.45.150(9) establishing a 0% contribution rate that supersedes the TRS employer UAAL-amortization rate from September 1, 2024 through August 31, 2029, a window that opens before the bill's own effective date of any later action and roughly a year ahead of the parallel PERS/SERS holidays.

Amends renumbered RCW 41.45.150(10) to direct the state actuary to review the appropriateness of "establishing, removing, or adjusting" minimum contribution rates (previously limited to reviewing existing minimum rates), broadening the recurring biennial review mandate.
Repeals uncodified 2021 c 334 s 747, a 2021 session-law provision whose substance is not reproduced in this bill's text.

pointsOfInterest: Converts an open-ended minimum-contribution floor tied to reaching 100% funded status into a fixed-term floor followed by a four-year 0% rate holiday for PERS 1/TRS 1 UAAL amortization -- a shift from funded-status-driven policy to calendar-driven policy, decoupling employer contribution relief from actual plan funding levels.

The TRS 0% holiday (RCW 41.45.150(9)) opens September 1, 2024, roughly a year ahead of the parallel PERS/PSERS holiday (July 1, 2025) and SERS holiday (September 1, 2025) -- an asymmetric schedule across systems sharing the same PERS 1/TRS 1 legacy liability that an analyst would want reconciled against each system's funded ratio.

Section 3 repeals a 2021 uncodified operating-budget proviso (2021 c 334 s 747) without stating its content anywhere in the bill -- typical of budget-conforming pension bills but it means the repealed policy can't be assessed from this text alone.

Section 1 quietly strips the "maximum" rate concept from the benefit-improvement amortization surcharge language in RCW 41.45.060(6)(c)/(7)(c)/(8)(c), leaving only an unbounded reference to RCW 41.45.150 rates -- a small drafting change that removes a prior cap concept and could matter if a future plan 1 benefit improvement's surcharge is no longer bounded by a maximum rate.

oneLine: HB 1279 amends the LEOFF definition of "firefighter" in RCW 41.26.030 to add a catch-all for full-time fire department employees in promotional positions requiring an experienced firefighter, so that firefighters who are promoted (e.g., to officer ranks not covered by the existing civil-service-exam or supervisory clauses) remain LEOFF members rather than falling out into PERS or another system.

provisions.detail: Inserts new RCW 41.26.030(17)(d), defining as a statutory "firefighter" any person serving full-time and fully compensated as an employee of a fire department in a position that requires an experienced firefighter, which keeps firefighters who accept promotional positions within LEOFF membership (plan 1 and plan 2 alike, since this new clause is not excluded from plan 2 the way several adjoining clauses are).

Relabels the existing firefighter-definition subsections (17)(d) through (h) as (e) through (i) to make room for the newly inserted (17)(d), a pure renumbering with no substantive change to those clauses' content.

Updates the internal cross-reference in the EMT-firefighter clause from RCW 18.73.030(12) to RCW 18.73.030(13), conforming to the renumbering already made by 2022 c 136 and flagged in the reviser's note; unrelated to the bill's stated policy purpose.

whoAffected: Firefighters who accept promotional (non-civil-service-exam) positions within a fire department; no member class loses eligibility
pointsOfInterest: The operative new language, "a position that requires an experienced firefighter," is undefined and untethered to civil service rank or job title, unlike every other clause in the (17) list, which invites administrative line-drawing by the Department of Retirement Systems over which promotional titles qualify and creates coverage-creep risk over time.

The new clause is not carved out of plan 2 the way the executive-secretary clauses in (17)(e)-(f) are, so it extends to both plan 1 and plan 2 members; keeping promoted staff in LEOFF rather than letting them fall to PERS preserves the employer's LEOFF 2 contribution obligation (a state-shared, statutorily set rate) rather than shifting cost to a different plan and rate structure.

The bill is a single-section, single-RCW-cite fix with no fiscal apparatus: no emergency clause, no null-and-void-without-appropriation language, and no retroactivity or contingent effective date, suggesting the drafters read this as closing a definitional gap rather than creating new liability.

A second, unrelated technical correction (updating an EMT cross-reference from RCW 18.73.030(12) to (13)) is bundled into the same already-amended section rather than left for a separate reviser's bill, a minor drafting economy rather than a substantive add.

oneLine: HB 1283 requires the Washington State Investment Board to publicly report every three years on climate-related financial risk and governance practices across its portfolios, and to offer at least three ESG-aligned investment options to plan 3 and self-directed program participants by January 1, 2024.

provisions.detail: Adds a new section to chapter 43.33A RCW requiring WSIB to publicly report by January 1, 2024, and every three years thereafter, on its analysis of climate-related financial risk, social responsibility, and proxy voting/corporate governance policy and use, across its private and public market portfolios, including alignment with the Paris climate agreement and the state climate commitment act.

Defines "climate-related financial risk" to include physical risks (storms, sea level rise, temperature) and transition risks (carbon emission costs, policy shifts, changing economics of carbon-intensive industries) for purposes of the new reporting mandate.

Reenacts and amends RCW 43.33A.190 to require that, beginning January 1, 2024, WSIB provide no fewer than three self-directed investment options consistent with the ESG policies examined under the new reporting section, reflecting a range of ESG-related policy preferences and investment objectives to the extent consistent with fiduciary duty.

whoAffected: Self-directed (defined contribution) account holders only: TRS plan 3, SERS plan 3, and PERS plan 3 members, plus WA ABLE program and (if selected) DreamAhead college savings program participants gain new ESG investment menu options; defined benefit plan members and non-self-directed portfolios are unaffected.
pointsOfInterest: This is a DC-menu-design and disclosure bill, not a benefit-design bill: it touches no multiplier, COLA, contribution rate, or funding policy, so its fiscal footprint is administrative (WSIB staff/reporting time and investment product development), not actuarial, despite the bill's pension classification.

The mandate reaches only self-directed plan 3 accounts (TRS/SERS/PERS 3), ABLE, and DreamAhead participants, not the far larger commingled DB trust funds where WSIB already reports it 'broadly incorporates' ESG considerations per the intent section, so the operative options requirement is a narrow slice of total WSIB-managed assets.

Section 3 reenacts and amends RCW 43.33A.190 citing two separate 2016 amendments to the same section (2016 c 69 s 20 and 2016 c 39 s 8), a code-reviser reconciliation of parallel 2016 changes rather than a substantive policy signal, but it adds drafting complexity worth checking against the current RCW text.

No emergency clause, no null-and-void-without-appropriation clause, and no contingent effective date despite a hard January 1, 2024 implementation deadline for both the report and the new investment options, so funding and timing risk for meeting that deadline is not addressed in the bill text itself.

oneLine: HB 1294 creates an annual CPI-indexed cost-of-living adjustment for TRS Plan 1 and PERS Plan 1 retirees, capped at 3 percent per year, with an emergency clause taking effect July 1, 2023.

provisions.detail: Adds a new section to chapter 41.32 RCW directing the department, beginning July 1, 2023 and annually thereafter, to compute a ratio-based COLA for each TRS Plan 1 retired member or beneficiary whose allowance has been in effect at least one year, using the ratio of CPI-W (Seattle area) for the year before determination to CPI-W for the year before July 1, 2022 (or the retirement date if later), applied against the original allowance as of June 30, 2023.
Identical new section added to chapter 41.40 RCW establishing the same ratio-based, CPI-W-indexed COLA mechanism for PERS Plan 1 retired members and beneficiaries.
Limits the new COLA to plan 1 retired members or beneficiaries whose retirement allowance has been in effect for at least one year at the time of determination.

Caps the adjustment so it can never reduce the allowance below the original amount, can never exceed 3 percent in the first annual adjustment, and cannot change from the prior year's adjustment by more than 3 percentage points.
Section 3 declares the act necessary for the immediate preservation of public peace, health, or safety and sets a fixed effective date of July 1, 2023, with no appropriation contingency attached.

whoAffected: TRS Plan 1 and PERS Plan 1 retirees and beneficiaries with at least one year on the retirement rolls; Plan 2/3 members and other retirement systems (LEOFF, WSPRS, SERS, etc.) are not touched.
pointsOfInterest: The formula duplicates the existing 'Uniform COLA' design already used elsewhere in the plan 2/3 systems (index-ratio to a base year, floor at original allowance, 3 percent annual cap), effectively extending that mechanism to the plan 1 cohort rather than inventing new COLA math.

No funding or appropriation provision accompanies the benefit increase; the bill carries an emergency clause and a fixed July 1, 2023 effective date rather than a contingent-on-appropriation clause, so enactment is not conditioned on the budget providing the money.

Because the year-over-year change is capped at 3 percentage points but the underlying ratio is measured against a fixed original-allowance base rather than compounding off the prior year's adjusted amount, a high-inflation stretch (2022 CPI was elevated) could produce a ratio above 3 percent that gets truncated in year one, with permanent under-indexing baked in if CPI outpaces the 3-point year-over-year cap in subsequent years.

Sections 1 and 2 are verbatim duplicates targeted at different chapters (41.32 for TRS, 41.40 for PERS), which is standard drafting practice for parallel plan 1 provisions but means any future amendment must be made in both places to stay in sync.

oneLine: SHB 1413 lets Washington law enforcement agencies adopt voluntary flexible/part-time work policies for peace officers and, by striking "full-time" from the officer definitions in RCW 41.26.030 (LEOFF) and RCW 10.93.020, opens LEOFF Plan 2 membership and peace-officer status to fully compensated officers who work less than full time, effective July 1, 2023.
whoAffected: General authority and limited authority Washington peace officers who are fully compensated but work part time (and the LEOFF employers that choose to use them); full-time officers, firefighters, and Plan 1 members are not directly affected by the definitional change.

provisions.detail: Adds new RCW 41.26.030(19)(f): beginning July 1, 2023, "law enforcement officer" also includes a person commissioned and employed on a fully compensated but less-than-full-time basis, so long as they meet the other qualifications in (a)-(e) of the subsection.
Conforming amendment to RCW 41.26.030(19)(c) states the full-time requirement for commissioned city police personnel does not apply to the extent allowed under new (19)(f).

Strikes "full-time," from the RCW 10.93.020 definitions of "general authority Washington peace officer" (4) and "limited authority Washington peace officer" (6), so part-time fully compensated officers qualify as peace officers for mutual-aid/commissioning purposes under chapter 10.93 RCW, not just for LEOFF.

Adds a new uncodified section to chapter 49.28 RCW authorizing (but not requiring) law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible/part-time work policies, barring layoff or displacement of full-time officers, preserving existing collective bargaining agreements and the duty to bargain, and requiring full-time and part-time officers at the same agency to be in the same bargaining unit.

Newly LEOFF-eligible part-time officers will accrue service credit under the existing Plan 2 hours-based partial-month schedule (full credit at 90+ hours/month, half credit at 70-89 hours, quarter credit below 70 hours); the bill does not create a new accrual rule for this group.

Updates an internal cross-reference in the emergency medical technician clause of the "firefighter" definition from RCW 18.73.030(12) to 18.73.030(13), a non-substantive recodification fix unrelated to the flexible-work policy.

pointsOfInterest: The membership expansion runs entirely through a definitional gateway (deleting "full-time" from RCW 41.26.030(19) and RCW 10.93.020) rather than a standalone eligibility or funding section, so its actuarial footprint depends on how many agencies actually adopt part-time policies under the new chapter 49.28 RCW authority - nothing in the bill text itself quantifies or caps that exposure.

No benefit formula, multiplier, vesting, or contribution-rate provision is touched; any cost effect is carried entirely through the existing Plan 2 hours-based partial service-credit schedule (quarter/half/full month), which was written for other purposes (e.g., mid-month hires, reduced schedules) and is now the mechanism by which a new class of intentionally part-time officers earns pension service.

"Beginning July 1, 2023" is embedded directly in the substantive definition (RCW 41.26.030(19)(f)) rather than set by a conventional bill effective-date section - an unusual drafting choice that, given this substitute's February 2023 first reading, could predate the bill's actual enactment and effective date, creating a quasi-retroactive application window for eligibility.

Section 1 is enabling only (agencies "may" adopt a flexible work policy) and explicitly forecloses a two-tier bargaining structure - full-time and part-time officers at the same employer must remain in the same bargaining unit - which limits the cost-shifting or labor-cost-arbitrage risk that a part-time carve-out might otherwise invite.

oneLine: HB 1459 grants PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 retirees a capped cost-of-living adjustment (3% per year, $110/month maximum increase) tied to the Seattle-area CPI, funded in part by only partially lowering the assumed long-term investment rate of return (from 7.7% to 7.2%, RCW 41.45.035), with an emergency clause and a legislative declaration that the act's provisions are nonseverable.

provisions.detail: Creates a new annual postretirement adjustment for TRS Plan 1 retirees/beneficiaries retired at least one year, based on the ratio of the current year's Seattle-area CPI to the CPI at retirement (or July 2022 base), applied each July.
provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.32 RCW

provisions.detail: Creates an identical new annual postretirement adjustment for PERS Plan 1 retirees/beneficiaries retired at least one year, using the same CPI-ratio methodology and same July effective date.
provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.40 RCW

provisions.detail: Caps the adjustment so it can never reduce the original allowance, cannot exceed 3 percent in the first year, cannot change by more than 3 percentage points from the prior year's adjustment, and cannot raise the monthly benefit by more than $110 over the prior year's amount.
provisions.cites: new sections to chapters 41.32 and 41.40 RCW

provisions.detail: States the legislature reserves the right to amend or repeal the new COLA provision at any time and that no member or beneficiary has a contractual right to an adjustment not already granted.
provisions.cites: new sections to chapters 41.32 and 41.40 RCW

provisions.detail: Amends the long-term investment rate of return assumption used by the state actuary, adding a new tier that lowers it from 7.7 percent (set in 2017) to 7.2 percent beginning July 1, 2023, a smaller reduction than the Pension Funding Council's 2021 recommendation of 7.0 percent.

Section 1 legislative findings declare the benefit increase and the investment rate of return change to be an integrated, nonseverable package, even though Section 5 contains a standard severability clause stating that if any provision is held invalid the remainder of the act stays in effect.

whoAffected: PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 retirees and beneficiaries who have been retired at least one year gain a capped CPI-linked COLA; PERS/TRS Plan 2 and 3 members and other retirement systems are unaffected, and all system members are affected indirectly through the changed investment return assumption used to value their plans.
pointsOfInterest: Section 1's uncodified findings assert the act's provisions are 'nonseverable,' but the operative Section 5 is a conventional severability clause preserving the rest of the act if any part is struck down — a direct textual conflict likely to draw scrutiny in any legal challenge.

The bill lowers the assumed investment rate of return only to 7.2 percent rather than the Pension Funding Council's recommended 7.0 percent, effectively pairing a smaller actuarial conservatism increase with the new COLA cost, a deliberate tradeoff flagged in the findings themselves.

The COLA is narrowly targeted: only Plan 1 members retired at least one year as of the July determination date qualify, and the $110/month and 3 percent caps mean the adjustment will lag actual CPI growth in high-inflation years, especially for higher-dollar allowances.

The 'no contractual right' / legislative reservation clause in both new sections signals this is designed as a discretionary, revocable benefit rather than a vested one, consistent with past legislative caution after Plan 1 COLA litigation history.

oneLine: HB 1481 lets Washington tribal governments elect, through a negotiated state-tribal compact, to enroll certificated general authority peace officers employed by tribal police departments in LEOFF Plan 2, with participating tribes paying both the employer and state contribution shares and a limited window to purchase prior service credit.

provisions.detail: Adds the government of a federally recognized tribe to the definition of a general authority law enforcement agency.

Adds a new subsection defining law enforcement officer to include a person employed on or after January 1, 2024 by a tribal police department under a section 2 compact who is certified as a general authority peace officer under chapter 43.101 RCW.
Renumbers a cross reference to RCW 18.73.030 from subsection (12) to (13), a conforming technical fix flagged by the reviser's note, not a substantive change.

Authorizes the governor to negotiate and execute state-tribal compacts admitting tribal general authority peace officers into LEOFF Plan 2, with an application process, a 90-day government-to-government meeting requirement, and mandatory compact terms covering employer status, reporting/contribution/auditing compliance, a limited waiver of sovereign immunity and consent to state court jurisdiction, dissolution and withdrawal-liability procedures, and acknowledgment of possible federal tax consequences.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 2)

provisions.detail: Provides that the pension-participation portions of a compact are null and void if the IRS finds them in conflict with governmental plan qualification requirements under IRC section 401(a) and the conflict cannot be resolved administratively or by amendment.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 2(6)(g))

provisions.detail: Provides that tribal law enforcement employees of a tribe that opts out of pension participation earn no service credit in the plan.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 2(7))

provisions.detail: Requires tribal governments participating through a state-tribal compact to contribute both the employer and state shares of retirement system cost for their LEOFF officers, the same funding obligation currently imposed on port districts and higher-education institutions.

Allows a tribal officer employed by a tribal police department on July 1, 2025 to purchase service credit for qualifying prior service, with a written election due by June 30, 2026 and full actuarial-cost payment required within five years of the election or before retirement, whichever comes first.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 4)

provisions.detail: Sets the act's effective date as July 1, 2025.

whoAffected: Certificated general authority peace officers employed full-time by tribal police departments of federally recognized tribes in Washington that opt into a state-tribal compact; a narrow new LEOFF Plan 2 membership class, with existing LEOFF 2 members and non-tribal employers otherwise unaffected.
pointsOfInterest: Creates a novel compact-based admission mechanism for a sovereign tribal government into a state pension system, including a negotiated limited waiver of tribal sovereign immunity and consent to state court jurisdiction for enforcement purposes, a precedent-setting design not used elsewhere in LEOFF.

Shifts the full funding burden onto participating tribes: RCW 41.26.450 makes tribal employers pay both the employer and the state contribution shares, unlike the normal three-way employee/employer/state split, so the state bears no ongoing normal-cost share for this new class.

Anticipates instability with explicit withdrawal-liability and dissolution procedures plus a null-and-void clause tied to future IRS guidance on IRC 401(a) governmental plan qualification, reflecting unresolved federal tax-law uncertainty about tribal government participation in a state retirement system.

Section 4's prior-service purchase window (elect by June 30, 2026, pay full actuarial cost) is self-funded by the member rather than subsidized, limiting cost/gaming risk to the plan, but the narrow eligibility date (must be employed on July 1, 2025) and short election window create a hard cutoff for who can buy in.

oneLine: HB 1566 raises the general state-employee vacation-leave accrual cap from 240 to 280 hours (RCW 43.01.040/.044) but freezes the PERS compensation-earnable exclusion and the termination cash-out cap at 240 hours, so the added leave does not flow into pensionable compensation, while adding a narrow WSPRS salary-exclusion fix for troopers commissioned before July 1, 2001.

provisions.detail: Raises the maximum accrued unused vacation leave a state officer/employee may carry from 240 to 280 hours (both the base cap and the extended cap available under a retained statement-of-necessity).

Conforms the alternative no-statement-of-necessity accumulation method's trigger threshold from 'in excess of 240 hours' to 'in excess of 280 hours,' matching the new base accrual cap in RCW 43.01.040.
Non-substantive drafting correction changing 'as [at] a minimum' to 'at a minimum' in the statement-of-necessity content requirements.

Adds an express cap limiting vacation-leave payout upon termination of employment to 'up to 240 hours,' even though the underlying accrual cap in RCW 43.01.040 is being raised to 280 hours, so up to 40 accrued hours become non-cashable at separation under this section.

Removes the cross-reference to RCW 43.01.044 and 43.01.041 from the PERS 'compensation earnable' exclusion for unused annual leave in excess of 240 hours, decoupling that pension-compensation exclusion threshold from the general leave statutes so a future change to the accrual/payout caps does not automatically alter what counts as pensionable compensation.

Converts numerous spelled-out numbers to numerals throughout the PERS definitions section (e.g., fifty-nine to 59, sixty to 60, twelve to 12, ten to 10, seventy to 70, twenty-two to 22, forty-five to 45, thirty-three to 33, eleven to 11) as non-substantive code-revision style cleanup with no benefit change.

Adds a new exclusion to the WSPRS 'salary' definition for members commissioned prior to July 1, 2001, excluding lump-sum payments for unused accumulated vacation or annual leave in excess of 240 hours (plus hours earned since the member's anniversary date) from countable salary, bringing that cohort into parity with the exclusion language already applicable to members commissioned on or after July 1, 2001.

whoAffected: All state officers and employees for general vacation-accrual purposes; PERS Plan 1/2/3 members and WSPRS Plan 1/2 members for the pension-compensation and cash-out provisions, with a narrow carve-out benefiting WSPRS members commissioned before July 1, 2001
pointsOfInterest: The bill raises the working accrual cap (240 to 280 hours) but deliberately holds the PERS compensation-earnable exclusion and the RCW 43.01.041 termination cash-out cap at 240 hours, an apparent anti-spiking design that expands a leave benefit without expanding pensionable compensation.

Severing the cross-reference in RCW 41.40.010(8)(a)(ii)(B) to RCW 43.01.044 and 43.01.041 is a notable drafting choice: it insulates the PERS compensation-earnable definition from future amendments to the general leave-accrual statutes, a precedent worth flagging for anyone tracking how pension definitions get decoupled from HR policy statutes.

The new WSPRS carve-out for members commissioned before July 1, 2001 is narrow and technical, but its existence implies that, absent this fix, that specific legacy cohort's salary definition may not have excluded large unused-leave cash-outs the way later cohorts' definitions already do, a potential prior spiking exposure for a small closed group.

The bulk of the RCW 41.40.010 changes are cosmetic numeral-for-spelled-number conversions, which could make the one substantive change in that section (the cross-reference removal in (8)(a)(ii)(B)) easy to overlook on a quick read.

oneLine: HB 1814 creates a new vaccination-mandate service-credit purchase right (up to five years) in LEOFF 2, TRS 2/3, SERS 2/3, PSERS, PERS 2/3, and WSPRS, adds a 10-point hiring-exam preference for employees separated over vaccination status, and takes effect immediately as an emergency measure.
whoAffected: Members of LEOFF Plan 2, TRS Plans 2/3, SERS Plans 2/3, PSERS, PERS Plans 2/3, and WSPRS Plan 2 who separated from public employment (voluntarily or involuntarily) due to an employer COVID-19 vaccination mandate imposed after January 1, 2020, and who later return to covered employment; also job applicants statewide who were dismissed for vaccination status.

provisions.detail: Adds a new subsection to RCW 41.26.520 (LEOFF 2) granting up to five years of retirement service credit for members who left employment, voluntarily or involuntarily, due to an employer vaccination mandate imposed after January 1, 2020.
Adds an identical vaccination-mandate service-credit purchase provision to RCW 41.32.810 (TRS 2/3 leave-of-absence/military service statute).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.32.865 (TRS defined-benefit/defined-contribution hybrid plan leave provisions).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.35.470 (SERS 2/3).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.35.650 (SERS Plan 3/hybrid leave provisions).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.37.260 (PSERS).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.40.710 (PERS 2).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.40.805 (PERS Plan 3 hybrid leave provisions).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 43.43.260 (WSPRS 2) and folds the new subsection into the existing 75 percent of average-final-salary benefit cap.

To claim the credit, a returning member must apply within 90 days of resuming covered employment and pay employee contributions (plus interest) within five years of resumption or before retirement, or, if those deadlines are missed, pay the alternative amount under RCW 41.50.165(2) prior to retirement.

Once the member pays the employee share, the administering department bills the former employer for its share of the plan-appropriate contributions (RCW 41.45.060, 41.45.061, and 41.45.067, or equivalent chapter cites) plus interest, for the separation period, shifting the employer contribution liability retroactively to employers who imposed the mandate.

Compensation used to calculate required contributions is the pay the member would have earned absent the mandate-related separation, or, if that cannot be reasonably estimated, the compensation reported for the member in the year before the separation (mirrors the existing military-leave compensation-estimation method).

New freestanding section adds a hiring preference in all state and local government (and contracted private) competitive civil-service examinations for applicants separated from any employment due to vaccination status in 2020-2022, adding 10 percent to the applicant's passing score.

Preference is self-certified: the applicant submits either proof of dismissal for vaccination status or proof of the prior employer's vaccination policy plus an affidavit of separation due to that policy; no independent verification mechanism is specified.

Legislative findings section recounts Executive Order 22-13's state workforce losses (about 1,900 employees including 400 transportation workers) and the state's subsequent shift from a vaccine-booster mandate to a $1,000 incentive payment, framing the bill's intent to facilitate rehiring and restore service credit.

pointsOfInterest: The employer contribution liability for the missed-service period is billed to the employer that imposed the mandate rather than shared prospectively across the plan, so the fiscal exposure lands narrowly on state agencies and local governments that had vaccination policies -- a targeted retroactive cost-shift rather than a systemwide funding change.

The bill defines the eligible population by a specific historical cause of separation (employer vaccination mandate after January 1, 2020) rather than by an ongoing plan feature, which is an unusual, one-time cohort carve-out layered into the general military-leave service-credit framework across nine separate RCW sections -- meaning any actuarial cost estimate depends entirely on how many separated employees actually return and buy back credit, a population that is hard to size ex ante.

The hiring-preference mechanism in the new chapter 41.04 section relies on applicant self-certification (affidavit plus policy proof) with no stated verification standard, which invites disputes over eligibility and potential inconsistency in how examining bodies apply the 10-point boost.

Six of nine amended sections are the DC/hybrid-plan leave-of-absence provisions (TRS/SERS/PERS Plan 3 and PSERS/WSPRS structures) where the mechanics of billing 'employer contributions' plus interest into a defined contribution account for a multi-year retroactive gap could pose administrative complications not present in straight defined-benefit plans.

The bill carries both an emergency clause and immediate effective date, atypical for a service-credit purchase bill of this kind, suggesting the sponsors intended fast implementation ahead of further changes to state vaccination policy referenced in the intent section.

oneLine: HB 1949 expands the PSERS Plan 2 "member" definition (RCW 41.37.010(19)(d)(iv)) to cover DSHS institutional/residential competency restoration workers who serve civilly committed residents or NGRI patients, and creates a new section letting current PERS Plan 2/3 employees at those sites elect, through September 1, 2025, to become PSERS Plan 2 dual members without transferring PERS service credit, while PERS Plan 1 members at those sites remain in Plan 1 and new hires are placed directly into PSERS.

provisions.detail: Amends the PSERS Plan 2 definition of "member" to add workers at DSHS/DCYF institutions or residential sites that serve civilly committed residents or patients found not guilty by reason of insanity, alongside the existing competency-restoration and developmentally-disabled categories (state-operated living alternatives facilities remain excluded).

Gives an employee who was in PERS Plan 2 or 3 immediately before the effective date and who meets the newly expanded eligibility criteria a one-time choice, during an election period running from the effective date to September 1, 2025, to stay in PERS or become a PSERS Plan 2 dual member under chapter 41.54 RCW.
provisions.cites: New section, chapter 41.37 RCW; chapter 41.54 RCW

provisions.detail: Bars transfer of service credit accrued in PERS into PSERS for employees who elect to switch; the PSERS membership is prospective only from the date of election.
Employees not electing by September 1, 2025 default to staying in their current PERS plan permanently, with no automatic PSERS conversion.
Employees who were PERS Plan 1 members on or before June 1, 2019 and later work in a newly eligible position remain in PERS Plan 1; they are not offered the PSERS election.
All new hires on or after the effective date who fill a newly eligible position become PSERS Plan 2 members automatically, with no election.
Sets the act's effective date at June 1, 2025, a year after the June 1, 2024 effective date of the underlying 2023 c 199 definitional section being amended.

whoAffected: DSHS/DCYF institutional and residential-site workers who provide custody, nursing, or security services to civilly committed residents or NGRI patients (competency restoration-adjacent staff), currently covered by PERS Plan 1, 2, or 3, gain PSERS Plan 2 eligibility; PERS Plan 1 members in that population are excluded from the new option and stay put.
pointsOfInterest: The mechanism is dual membership under ch. 41.54 RCW with no PERS-to-PSERS service credit transfer, so the bill avoids shifting accrued PERS liability onto PSERS; the actuarial cost is limited to prospective service and any dual-membership benefit calculation effects, not a stock of transferred credit.

PERS Plan 1 members are affirmatively locked out of the election and must remain in Plan 1, consistent with the closed, legislatively protected status of Plan 1 and avoidance of moving Plan 1's distinct funding and benefit structure into PSERS.

A roughly 15-month, one-time election window (effective date to September 1, 2025) is a self-selection design: analysts would expect adverse selection toward PSERS by employees for whom the more generous PSERS 2%/60 formula and earlier retirement age outweigh PERS terms, which OSA would need to model as a participation-rate assumption rather than a known cost.

Eligibility turns on fact-specific site/duty classifications ("serve civilly committed residents," "serve patients under not guilty by reason of insanity findings") layered onto existing competency-restoration language; boundary calls about which specific institutions or rotating staff qualify could generate classification disputes similar to those seen in other PSERS carve-outs.

oneLine: SHB 1985 extends the annual one-time ad hoc benefit increase for TRS Plan 1 and PERS Plan 1 retirees by adding a fifth increment: beneficiaries on the rolls as of July 1, 2023 get a 3 percent increase, capped at $110/month, effective July 1, 2024.

provisions.detail: Adds new subsection (5) to RCW 41.32.4992 granting TRS Plan 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2023 a 3 percent increase to that benefit, capped at $110.00, effective July 1, 2024.

Adds new subsection (5) to RCW 41.40.1987 granting PERS Plan 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2023 a 3 percent increase to that benefit, capped at $110.00, effective July 1, 2024.
Renumbers the exclusion clause as subsection (6) and retains that the TRS increase does not apply to those receiving benefits under RCW 41.32.489 or 41.32.540.
Renumbers the exclusion clause as subsection (6) and retains that the PERS increase does not apply to those receiving benefits under RCW 41.40.1984.

whoAffected: Retirees and beneficiaries of TRS Plan 1 and PERS Plan 1 who were on the benefit rolls as of July 1, 2023, excluding those already receiving benefits under the separate minimum-benefit provisions of RCW 41.32.489, 41.32.540, and 41.40.1984.
pointsOfInterest: This is the fifth consecutive one-time, non-compounding ad hoc increase layered onto closed Plan 1 systems (2018, 2020, 2022, 2023, now 2024), each keyed to a snapshot date of who is on the rolls, rather than an ongoing COLA; the dollar cap has been frozen at $110 for three cycles running, so the cap itself has not kept pace with inflation.

The bill continues the pattern set by 2023 c 397, whose uncodified finding stated an ongoing COLA "may not be affordable until required employer contribution rates towards the unfunded accrued actuarial liability are reduced or no longer required" and directed SCPP to study a permanent COLA during the 2023-25 biennium; this bill enacts another one-time patch rather than the studied permanent fix, leaving that study mandate unresolved.

No emergency clause and no null-and-void-without-appropriation clause appear in this bill's own text, unlike its 2023 c 397 predecessor which carried an immediate-effective-date emergency clause; worth confirming the bill's effective date against its internal July 1, 2024 trigger date.

Eligibility is a point-in-time snapshot (on the rolls as of July 1, 2023) rather than continuous eligibility through the effective date, which is standard for this series but worth checking against survivor benefit rules for any edge-case windfalls if status changes between snapshot and effective date.

oneLine: HB 2013 adds a new section to chapter 41.50 RCW directing DRS to continue paying retiree and beneficiary benefits through the end of the month in which death occurs (rather than stopping on the exact death date), delays survivor benefits to the first of the following month, preserves DRS's authority to recover payments issued after month-end, and bars retroactive refund claims for repayments already made before the January 1, 2025 effective date.

provisions.detail: Requires DRS to continue paying retiree or beneficiary benefits through the end of the month in which death occurs, rather than stopping precisely on the date of death, across all listed retirement systems.
provisions.cites: New section, chapter 41.50 RCW; applies to retirees/beneficiaries under chapters 2.10, 2.12, 41.26, 41.32, 41.35, 41.37, 41.40, and 43.43 RCW

provisions.detail: Sets the start date for survivor benefits at the first day of the month following the month in which the retiree or beneficiary died, coordinating with the new month-end payment rule.
Clarifies that the month-end payment rule applies to all benefit payments issued by DRS, including optional annuities, not just standard periodic retirement allowances.

Preserves DRS's existing authority and obligation to require the beneficiary, survivor, or estate to refund any benefit payments issued for periods after the month of death, so the fix shifts the recovery cutoff to month-end but does not eliminate overpayment recovery.
Makes the new rule prospective only, expressly stating that no beneficiary, survivor, or estate that repaid benefits before January 1, 2025 has any right to a refund of those prior repayments.

whoAffected: Retirees, beneficiaries, survivors, and estates across essentially all state retirement systems (PERS, TRS, SERS/PSERS, LEOFF, WSPRS, and judicial retirement under chapters 2.10, 2.12, 41.26, 41.32, 41.35, 41.37, 41.40, and 43.43 RCW) whose death occurs mid-month; estates of decedents dying mid-month gain a partial month of retained benefits, while estates of those who already repaid pre-2025 overpayments gain nothing.
pointsOfInterest: A single new section in chapter 41.50 RCW (the general DRS administration chapter) reaches into eight separate retirement-system chapters at once, rather than amending each system's statute individually, a centralization approach rather than parallel system-by-system amendments.

Subsection (4) affirmatively forecloses refund claims from estates that already repaid pre-2025 overpayments under the old date-of-death cutoff, a defensive drafting choice that limits the state's retroactive liability exposure rather than extending equitable relief to past cases.

The bill does not eliminate DRS's overpayment recovery power; subsection (3) keeps clawback authority intact for payments beyond the new month-end cutoff, so the change is narrowly a shift in the cutoff date, not a broader forgiveness of overpayments.

By request of the Select Committee on Pension Policy (SCPP), signaling this originated as a technical administrative-correction bill rather than a benefit-expansion policy initiative, consistent with its narrow, mechanical scope.

oneLine: 2SHB 2014 broadens Washington's statutory definition of "veteran" to reach general-under-honorable, other-than-honorable-with-VA-benefits, and LGBTQ+ bias discharges across dozens of licensing, tuition, employment, and benefit statutes, but deliberately excludes PERS and old-law police/fire pension military service credit from that broadened standard, and makes the entire act null and void absent a 2024 appropriation.
whoAffected: Veterans/former service members with general-under-honorable, other-than-honorable (VA-benefit-eligible), or LGBTQ+ bias-motivated discharges gain expanded state licensing, tuition, hunting/fishing, employment-preference, and veterans'-home benefits; the same members are excluded from gaining expanded PERS/old-law police and fire pension military service credit, which retains the narrower honorable-discharge/period-of-war standard.

provisions.detail: Creates a new statutory "qualifying discharge" definition (new section, ch. 73.04 RCW) that includes honorable, general-under-honorable, other-than-honorable-with-VA-monetary-benefits, and any discharge motivated solely by sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression (or related statements/conduct/disclosure), and applies it across roughly 19 cross-referenced RCW sections governing licensing, tuition, hunting/fishing, gambling-license renewal, and civil-service employment preference.

Strikes the cross-reference to RCW 41.16.220, 41.20.050, and 41.40.170 from the RCW 41.04.005 "veteran" definition being broadened, and instead rewrites those three sections to spell out "honorably discharged" (or honorable-record physical discharge) with period-of-war service directly, so PERS and old-law police/fire pension military service-credit purchase does not inherit the act's broadened qualifying-discharge standard.

Reenacts and amends RCW 41.40.170 (PERS military service credit purchase) to require the member be "an honorably discharged veteran or veteran who received a physical discharge from the armed forces with an honorable record" and to affirmatively prove period-of-war service under RCW 41.04.005, tightening the drafting even as it fixes an internal citation error (41.40.005 to 41.04.005).

Reenacts and amends RCW 41.20.050 (old-law city police pension) to require honorable discharge (or honorable-record physical discharge) during a period of war for military-service credit toward the 25-year pension calculation.

Amends RCW 84.39.020 to allow the deceased-veteran property tax exemption for surviving spouses even where the veteran had an other-than-honorable discharge, provided the veteran or survivor was eligible for or received federal VA monetary benefits.

Amends RCW 28B.15.012 to apply the qualifying-discharge standard to resident-tuition eligibility for veterans and their dependents, while retaining exclusion of students with bad-conduct discharge, officer dismissal, or dishonorable discharge.

Repeals RCW 2.48.100 (bar admission, effect of disability discharge) and RCW 73.04.042 (1919/1923 honorable-discharge recording statute for Spanish-American War and WWI veterans) as obsolete honorable-discharge-based provisions superseded by the qualifying-discharge standard.
Adds a new section directing the Department of Veterans Affairs to develop and implement an outreach program informing veterans of the law's changes, beginning on that section's effective date.

pointsOfInterest: The bill's headline reform (a broadened "qualifying discharge" standard reaching LGBTQ+ bias discharges and other-than-honorable-with-VA-benefits cases) is deliberately not extended to RCW 41.40.170 (PERS military service credit) or RCW 41.20.050/41.16.220 (predecessor police/fire pension military credit) — Sec. 2 strips those three RCW cites from the definition's scope and Secs. 18-20 restate "honorably discharged"/period-of-war language directly, so bad-paper veterans gain tuition, licensing, and hunting benefits but not retirement service credit purchase eligibility.

Section 40 makes the entire act null and void without a specific appropriation identified by bill or chapter number in the omnibus budget by June 30, 2024 — a funding contingency that would also nullify the pension-carve-out drafting itself if unfunded.

Section 37 exempts the act from the tax-preference performance-statement/JLARC automatic-review requirements (RCW 82.32.805/.808), even though Sec. 36 touches a property-tax exemption (RCW 84.39.020) for veterans' widows — a drafting choice that avoids future sunset review of that tax provision.

Sections 24-27 (armed-forces, Purple Heart, and Pearl Harbor license plates, and veterans emblems) get a staggered April 1, 2025 contingent effective/expiration date decoupled from the rest of the act, apparently for DOL system lead time; RCW 41.40.170's retroactive-recalculation note (from a prior 2023 act, not this bill) continues to reference the older, narrower veteran definition since 41.40.170 was excluded from the broadened standard.

oneLine: HB 2024 authorizes law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible/part-time work policies for peace officers and, in the companion definitional amendments, opens LEOFF Plan 2 "law enforcement officer" membership to fully compensated but less-than-full-time officers beginning July 1, 2024, while expressly excluding reserve peace officers called into active service.

provisions.detail: Adds a new section to chapter 49.28 RCW authorizing (not requiring) general and limited authority Washington law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible/part-time work policies, subject to no displacement of full-time officers, no alteration of existing collective bargaining agreements or duty-to-bargain obligations, and a requirement that full-time and part-time officers in the same bargaining unit be covered together.

Strikes the 'full-time,' qualifier from the definitions of 'general authority Washington peace officer' and 'limited authority Washington peace officer,' extending those statuses (used for mutual aid and commissioning purposes) to part-time commissioned officers.

In the pre-July 1, 2025 version of the LEOFF definitions section, strikes 'full time' from the city-police-officer qualifier and adds new subsection (19)(g) providing that 'law enforcement officer' does not include reserve peace officers called into active service under RCW 10.93.020.

Adds new subsection (19)(h) to the pre-July 1, 2025 version of RCW 41.26.030 making a person commissioned and fully compensated, but working less than full time, a 'law enforcement officer' eligible for LEOFF Plan 2 membership beginning July 1, 2024.

Makes the parallel amendment (reserve-officer exclusion at new (19)(g) and part-time officer inclusion at new (19)(h)) to the post-July 1, 2025 version of RCW 41.26.030, which already incorporates the 2023 c 77 tribal-police-officer membership provision, so the part-time definition carries forward without a gap.

Sunsets the temporary Section 3 version of RCW 41.26.030 on July 1, 2025, and makes the parallel Section 4 version effective the same date, synchronizing the part-time officer definition with the already-scheduled tribal officer amendment.

whoAffected: Part-time (less-than-full-time), fully compensated commissioned peace officers of general and limited authority Washington law enforcement agencies gain LEOFF Plan 2 "law enforcement officer" eligibility; reserve peace officers called into active service are expressly excluded from LEOFF membership status.
pointsOfInterest: The bill text contains no actuarial or fiscal adjustment language, yet it expands the LEOFF Plan 2 covered population to a new class of part-time officers; an OSA reader would look for the accompanying fiscal note rather than the bill itself for cost impact to the tri-party (state/employer/employee) funded plan.

The eligibility expansion is threaded twice, into both the pre- and post-July 1, 2025 versions of RCW 41.26.030 (Sec. 3 and Sec. 4), using an expire/take-effect pairing (Sec. 5, Sec. 6) to keep the temporary and permanent versions in sync with the already-scheduled 2023 c 77 tribal-officer amendment; any future drafter who amends only one version risks the two falling out of alignment.

The reserve-officer exclusion is a narrow carve-out drawn specifically to prevent reserve peace officers called into active duty under chapter 10.93 RCW from being swept into LEOFF membership by the new part-time officer language, forestalling an unintended eligibility expansion to a much larger and more casual class of personnel.

The flexible-work-policy authorization (Sec. 1, chapter 49.28 RCW) is a labor-policy provision layered loosely onto the pension eligibility change via a shared definitions cross-reference (RCW 10.93.020); an agency can adopt a flexible work policy without necessarily triggering the LEOFF membership question, and existing LEOFF Plan 2 service-credit tiers (70/90-hour monthly thresholds) already accommodate part-time work, so the practical benefit-computation mechanics for final average salary during transitions between full-time and part-time status are not separately addressed.

oneLine: HB 2167 lets LEOFF 2 retirees who have separated from service for six months or more return to part-time LEOFF officer/firefighter work (up to 1040 hours per year, for up to three years) without suspension of their retirement allowance, while forgoing further service credit, and adds a statutory definition of "separation from service" tied to the anti-collusion return-to-work rule in RCW 41.26.062.

provisions.detail: Adds new subsection (4) to RCW 41.26.500 allowing a LEOFF 2 retiree who has separated from service for six months or more to work in an eligible LEOFF position for up to 1040 hours per calendar year for up to three years without suspension of the monthly retirement allowance.
Retirees using the new part-time return-to-work window forgo any service credit or other accrual of retirement benefits for hours worked during that period.

The bill expressly states the expanded postretirement work eligibility is not a contractual right and may be repealed or modified by the legislature at any time, a non-vesting disclaimer aimed at avoiding contract-clause protection under state pension case law.

Adds new definition (29) "Separation from service," specifying it occurs only when a person has terminated all employment with an employer, and that a written or oral agreement to resume employment with the same employer defeats separation and may violate the bona fide separation rule in RCW 41.26.062.

Because RCW 41.26.030 is already scheduled to be amended by 2023 c 77 effective July 1, 2025 (adding tribal police department officers to the "law enforcement officer" definition), the bill amends both the pre- and post-July 1, 2025 versions of the section in parallel to keep the new "separation from service" definition and renumbering consistent across both.

Sections 4 and 5 sunset the pre-July 1, 2025 version of the definitions section (Section 1) and set the effective date of the post-July 1, 2025 version (Section 2) to July 1, 2025, matching the existing 2023 c 77 schedule.

whoAffected: LEOFF Plan 2 retirees who separate from service for six months or more and their rehiring LEOFF employers; no change for LEOFF Plan 1 members or non-LEOFF retirement systems
pointsOfInterest: The 1040-hour/three-year return-to-work window lets a retiree draw a full pension and a part-time LEOFF paycheck simultaneously; benefit-formula spiking is blocked by the service-credit forgo clause, but the policy still raises the classic double-dipping optics/cost question OSA typically flags even where the funding math is neutral.

The new 'separation from service' definition is deliberately cross-referenced to the pre-arranged-return prohibition in RCW 41.26.062, suggesting drafters are threading a six-month bright-line rule around an existing anti-collusion standard rather than replacing it; the interaction between the two provisions is left for DRS to administer.

The non-contractual-right disclaimer in new RCW 41.26.500(4)(c) is unusual and purposeful drafting, an explicit attempt to keep this benefit outside the vested-rights doctrine that has otherwise made Washington pension liberalizations hard to unwind.

The double amendment of RCW 41.26.030 (Sections 1 and 2, with Sections 4 and 5 as bridging sunset/effective-date sections) is a technical artifact of a second pending bill (2023 c 77) already scheduled to take effect July 1, 2025; it is clean drafting but signals the section is a live target for multiple bills in the same biennium.

oneLine: SHB 2152 is a 55-section terminology overhaul of Washington's criminal-insanity and competency-to-stand-trial statutes (replacing "incompetent"/"competency" language with "unable to proceed to trial due to a mental health condition" and similar person-first phrasing); its only PSERS touchpoint is a nominal relabeling of "competency restoration services" to "restoration treatment services" within the RCW 41.37.010 Plan 2 membership definition, with an accompanying savings clause stating the act changes no substantive meaning.
whoAffected: PSERS Plan 2 members employed at DSHS/DCYF institutions (juvenile rehabilitation facilities, mental health hospitals, child study and treatment centers) whose duties include custody/security for patients undergoing what the statute now calls "restoration treatment" rather than "competency restoration"; the covered class of employees is unchanged.

provisions.detail: Renames "competency restoration services" to "restoration treatment services" within the PSERS Plan 2 "member" definition covering staff at state institutions who provide custody/security for offender, probationary, or patient populations, or perform those services; no change to which job classes or institutions qualify.

Uncodified savings clause states the act's terminology amendments are not intended to change the substantive meaning of the underlying concepts and do not alter the applicability or effect of prior case law on criminal insanity or inability to proceed to trial.

Sets a contingent effective date tying two unrelated civil-commitment definitions to a prior act's trigger; this contingency does not apply to the PSERS section (Sec. 39), which takes effect on the bill's normal effective date.

pointsOfInterest: Of 55 amended/reenacted sections, only one (RCW 41.37.010) touches a retirement statute; the PSERS classification rests entirely on a single incidental relabeling inside a criminal-justice terminology bill, not on any deliberate pension policy change.

The bill carries its own savings clause (Sec. 57) disclaiming substantive effect, which is unusually explicit reassurance for a bill coded as pension-related — useful for an analyst confirming zero actuarial or eligibility impact rather than inferring it from silence.

RCW 41.37.010 is amended "as amended by 2023 c 199 s 3," a very recent companion act (2023 telecommunicator PERS/PSERS expansion); layering a terminology-only edit on top of a just-enacted substantive amendment raises an ordinary but nontrivial code-reviser sequencing/publication risk.

No cost-shifting, contribution-rate, multiplier, or membership-count effect is created; this is the rare "pension bill" that an OSA fiscal note would properly score as zero fiscal impact despite touching an RCW that defines a covered retirement plan's membership.

oneLine: HB 2316 amends RCW 41.40.023 to add a new, narrow PERS membership exclusion for part-time bus drivers on naval-shipyard routes for a public transportation benefit area who are simultaneously full-time federal employees contributing to the federal retirement system, plus carries two unrelated technical conforming edits in the same section.

provisions.detail: Adds new membership exception (23): persons hired on or after the effective date, employed by a public transportation benefit area (RCW 36.57A.010) as part-time bus drivers serving naval shipyards, are excluded from mandatory PERS membership if they are simultaneously employed full-time by an employer of the federal government and making contributions to the federal employees' retirement system.

Technical conforming amendment splitting the reference to the former combined 'volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund' into the two separate funds created by 2023 c 73, with no substantive policy effect.
Technical renaming of the 'liquor control board' to the 'liquor and cannabis board' to conform to the 2015 rename, no substantive policy effect.

whoAffected: A narrow class of part-time bus drivers for a public transportation benefit area serving naval shipyard routes who are also full-time federal government employees (e.g., federal civilian shipyard workers driving a shuttle route, likely Kitsap Transit serving Puget Sound Naval Shipyard) lose PERS membership eligibility for that part-time job; other listed exception classes are unaffected in substance.
pointsOfInterest: The new provision is an exclusion from membership, not an expansion of access: it relieves the transit employer of PERS employer contributions for these part-time drivers, while the drivers forgo any PERS service credit for that job, in exchange for avoiding simultaneous participation in two retirement systems for overlapping employment.

The carve-out is unusually specific in both geography and employment structure (part-time bus driver, naval shipyard route, employer is a public transportation benefit area, employee also full-time federal and contributing to FERS), suggesting the bill was drafted to fit one identifiable real-world workforce (transit agency shuttle drivers serving a naval shipyard) rather than a general policy class.

No fiscal note language, actuarial impact statement, or SCPP analysis is present in the bill text itself; given the request-of-SCPP sponsorship, the class size is presumably small enough that any PERS trust fund impact would be treated as negligible, but that determination is not visible from the text.

Two unrelated technical/reviser cleanup edits (firefighters' fund split, liquor board rename) are bundled into the same amendatory section as the substantive change, typical drafting practice when reopening a frequently-amended RCW section but worth separating out when assessing what the bill actually does.

oneLine: HB 2246 raises the general state employee vacation-accrual cap from 240 to 280 hours (RCW 43.01.040/.044) and makes conforming amendments to PERS plan 1 and WSPRS plan 1 compensation definitions so the added leave does not translate into higher pension-computable pay, including a new anti-spiking exclusion for a narrow class of WSPRS officers commissioned before July 1, 2001.

provisions.detail: Raises the maximum accrual of unused vacation leave for state officers and employees from 240 to 280 hours, and correspondingly raises the cap that applies when leave use is deferred and extended by statement of necessity.

Conforms the alternative no-statement-of-necessity vacation accumulation method to the new 280-hour threshold (three references changed from 240 to 280 hours); leaves intact the existing rule that this alternative accumulation shall not increase a retirement allowance under any public retirement system.

Removes the cross-reference to RCW 43.01.044 and 43.01.041 in the PERS plan 1 definition of compensation earnable while leaving the exclusion of remuneration for unused annual leave in excess of 240 hours unchanged, meaning the compensation-earnable exclusion threshold was not raised to match the new 280-hour accrual cap.

Adds a new exclusion to the WSPRS plan 1 definition of pension-computable salary for lump sum payments for unused accumulated vacation or annual leave in excess of 240 hours (plus hours earned since the member's anniversary date), applicable only to members commissioned before July 1, 2001, a group whose salary definition previously did not exclude such payments unlike the two later-commissioned cohorts.

Makes numerous nonsubstantive numeral-style edits converting spelled-out numbers to digits (e.g., sixty to 60, twelve to 12, seventy to 70) throughout the PERS definitions section, with no effect on benefits.

whoAffected: All state civil-service employees (higher vacation accrual cap); PERS plan 1 members and, narrowly, WSPRS plan 1 members commissioned before July 1, 2001 (pension compensation-definition conformance/anti-spiking fix)
pointsOfInterest: The bill's operative policy change (240 to 280 hour vacation cap) sits in Title 43.01, a personnel statute; three of its four sections instead amend PERS and WSPRS compensation definitions purely to keep the larger leave balance from flowing into pension-computable pay, i.e., this is fundamentally an anti-spiking conforming bill riding alongside an HR leave-policy change.

Sec. 3 strips the RCW 43.01.044/.041 cross-reference from the PERS plan 1 compensation-earnable exclusion but leaves the numeric threshold at 240 hours rather than updating it to 280; still protective in effect (anything paid above 240 hours stays excluded), but the mismatch between the new 280-hour accrual cap and the still-240-hour compensation exclusion is a drafting artifact worth flagging.

Sec. 4 creates a genuinely narrow carve-out: the added salary exclusion applies only to WSPRS officers commissioned before July 1, 2001, a closed and shrinking cohort nearing or past retirement eligibility, apparently closing a gap because later-commissioned cohorts already had this exclusion in their salary definitions.

No emergency clause, no null-and-void-without-appropriation clause, and no contingent effective date appear anywhere in the bill, consistent with the drafters treating this as fiscally neutral -- the existing 'shall not result in any increase in a retirement allowance' savings clause in RCW 43.01.044(3) is left undisturbed.

oneLine: HB 2337 exempts LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board employees from civil service coverage and gives the board direct authority to hire staff outside Title 41 RCW and set their salaries, downgrading OFM's role from consultation to mere notice.

provisions.detail: Adds employees of the LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board to the list of positions exempt from classified civil service coverage under the state civil service law.

Removes the existing requirement that LEOFF 2 board staff (other than the executive director) be state employees under Title 41 RCW, instead authorizing the board itself to set staff salaries subject to periodic board review.

Changes the process for setting the executive director's salary: the board must now merely provide notice to the OFM director rather than consult with OFM, while continuing to notify the house and senate fiscal committee chairs of changes.

whoAffected: Staff and executive director of the LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board (a small administrative body), who gain hiring/compensation autonomy; OFM loses its consultative role over executive salary-setting.
pointsOfInterest: The carve-out affects an extremely small class (the board's own staff, likely fewer than a dozen positions), the kind of narrow personnel-law exemption that draws little floor debate but sets durable precedent.

Removing the Title 41 RCW state-employee requirement lets the board hire and pay staff outside the classified civil service and general state salary schedules, mirroring autonomy already granted to entities like the state investment board; this is a governance template other retirement boards could later seek.

Downgrading OFM's role from 'consultation with' to 'notice to' on executive director salary-setting reduces centralized executive-branch oversight of compensation, shifting effective control to the board and legislative fiscal committees (notice only, not approval).

The bill is by request of the LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board itself, i.e., a governance/HR housekeeping measure originating from the board rather than OSA or SCPP, with no apparent fiscal note implications for plan funding, benefits, or contribution rates.

oneLine: HB 2338 removes the statute of limitations on LEOFF special death benefit claims and creates a retroactive reopening path for previously denied beneficiaries, shifts liability for employer-caused LEOFF 2 pension overpayments from retirees to employers (capped at one year absent fraud), modestly broadens the firefighter definition, and lets certain nonduty PTSD disability retirees seek retroactive reclassification to line-of-duty status as L&I's occupational-disease determinations evolve.

provisions.detail: Eliminates the statute of limitations on the LEOFF special death benefit and requires L&I to redetermine eligibility for beneficiaries previously denied solely for missing that deadline, with an option to reelect an ongoing pension under RCW 41.26.510(2) paid retroactive to the member's death.

Expands the statutory definition of 'firefighter' to add full-time, fully compensated fire department personnel in positions that necessitate firefighter experience to perform essential job functions, with conforming subsection reletterings.

Makes the identical firefighter-definition addition to the parallel, later-effective version of the same definitions section that already incorporates the 2023 tribal-officer and general-authority-agency language, via a synchronized expiration/effective-date pair (Sec. 201 expires 7/1/2025; Sec. 202 takes effect 7/1/2025) so the change survives the scheduled 2023 c 77 amendment.

Provides that a LEOFF 2 retiree is not liable to repay a pension overpayment caused by an employer's erroneous reporting of member information (absent member nondisclosure, fraud, or misrepresentation), and exempts such employer-caused overpayments from the standard three-year lookback limit on benefit corrections.
