Creates a new section making the employer liable to reimburse the LEOFF 2 retirement fund for overpayments caused by the employer's erroneous reporting, with liability capped at one year of overpayments plus interest unless the employer committed fraud, in which case the employer is liable for the full overpayment; effective January 1, 2025.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 302); Sec. 303

provisions.detail: Allows a member receiving a nonduty disability benefit for a condition not classified as an occupational disease at the time of retirement, but now meeting the PTSD occupational-disease definition, to file a new application for a line-of-duty disability determination, with the higher benefit paid retroactive to the date the condition became eligible as an occupational disease.

whoAffected: LEOFF Plan 2 active members, retirees, beneficiaries, and their employers, with the death-benefit statute-of-limitations fix also reaching past-denied beneficiaries chapter-wide and a narrow class of nonduty PTSD disability retirees gaining a reclassification path
pointsOfInterest: Sec. 101(3) reopens denied special-death-benefit claims with no dollar cap or outer time bound on the retroactive pension payments, creating open-ended liability exposure tied to a claims-processing failure rather than a benefit design change.

Sec. 302 is a cost-shift from members to employers for employer reporting errors, but the one-year cap (absent fraud) means older employer-caused overpayments still fall back on the fund/member, only partially transferring the liability.

Sec. 401(12) ties a retroactive disability-reclassification right to L&I's evolving occupational-disease determinations for PTSD, meaning future L&I policy changes could retroactively convert an unknown, currently-unquantifiable number of nonduty retirements into higher-cost line-of-duty retirements.

The twin-section drafting for RCW 41.26.030 (Secs. 201-204) is pension-code bookkeeping to synchronize with a previously enacted, not-yet-effective 2023 amendment rather than a substantive change in itself, and is easy to misread as two separate policy changes.

oneLine: Creates a time-limited (through June 30, 2029) $15,000 annual longevity bonus for Washington State Patrol commissioned employees with 26+ years of service, statutorily excluded from salary and average final salary for pension calculation purposes, contingent on collective bargaining agreement changes, with a mandated 2028 JLARC performance review.

provisions.detail: Creates a new state trooper longevity bonus of $15,000 annually, paid on the employee's state-service anniversary date, for eligible commissioned employees with 26 or more years of service, beginning July 1, 2024.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 43.43 RCW (Sec. 2(1), (6))

provisions.detail: Establishment of the bonus is made subject to negotiated changes in the applicable collective bargaining agreements with the exclusive bargaining representatives, and the section expressly disclaims any interference with collective bargaining rights under RCW 41.56.473.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 43.43 RCW (Sec. 2(2), (3)); RCW 41.56.473

provisions.detail: Declares the bonus a time-limited incentive not intended to be included in salary or average final salary for pension benefit calculations, and states it is not a matter of contractual right, so the legislature may alter or abolish it at any time.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 43.43 RCW (Sec. 2(4), (5))

provisions.detail: The new bonus section itself expires June 30, 2029, sunsetting the pilot program.
provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 43.43 RCW (Sec. 2(7))

provisions.detail: Amends the WSPRS definition of 'salary' for all three commissioning-date tiers to expressly exclude earnings from the new longevity bonus, preventing the bonus from inflating average final salary and retirement allowances.

Converts several spelled-out numbers in the WSPRS definitions section (e.g., 'seventy' to '70,' 'sixty' to '60,' 'twelve' to '12,' 'seventy-seven' to '77') to numerals; a non-substantive drafting cleanup riding along with the salary amendment.
Section 3 (the RCW 43.43.120 amendment carrying the salary exclusion) is itself set to expire June 30, 2029, tying the salary-exclusion language to the same sunset as the bonus program.

Requires the joint legislative audit and review committee to complete a performance review of the longevity bonus pilot by November 1, 2028, assessing retention impact, vacancy trends, optimal staffing levels compared to other states, and other retention factors, and to recommend whether to continue the program; this review section also expires June 30, 2029.

whoAffected: Washington State Patrol commissioned employees (troopers/sergeants) in the Washington State Patrol Retirement System with 26 or more years of service; no other WSPRS members or classes are affected.
pointsOfInterest: The bonus is deliberately walled off from pension calculations: Sec. 2(4) and the parallel amendments to the 'salary' definition in RCW 43.43.120(21)(a)-(c) both exclude the $15,000 payment from average final salary, an explicit anti-spiking design choice for what is otherwise a large annual payment to a senior, near-retirement cohort.

The entire program is a five-year pilot: the new benefit section, the salary-exclusion amendment (via a separate standalone Sec. 5 expiration section), and the JLARC review mandate all sunset June 30, 2029, with the review due by November 1, 2028 to inform a continuation decision.

Eligibility is unusually narrow and senior: 26+ years of service (beyond the roughly 25-year mark the findings cite for 122 currently retirement-eligible staff), targeting retention of the most senior commissioned staff specifically to preserve a leadership pipeline, rather than addressing broader recruitment or mid-career retention.

The bonus's actual establishment is made contingent on collective bargaining agreement changes (Sec. 2(2)), and the bill preserves the legislature's unilateral right to alter or abolish it (Sec. 2(5)) with no contractual right created, standard non-vesting boilerplate that keeps this off the books as a pension enhancement despite its size and recurrence.

oneLine: HB 2405 directs WSIB to integrate climate and other sustainability factors into investment decision-making, adopt proxy voting guidelines favoring climate-risk-reducing shareholder resolutions, report annually on environmental sustainability of its investment process, and requires a state auditor evaluation of proxy voting conformance every two years starting December 2027.

provisions.detail: Adds subsection requiring the board to integrate sustainability factors (governance, environmental, social, human capital) into its investment decision making, analysis, portfolio construction, due diligence, and ownership when determining a prudent level of risk.

Enumerates a non-exhaustive list of sustainability factors the board should strive to incorporate when updating sustainability frameworks, covering corporate governance/leadership, environmental, social capital, human capital, and business model/innovation categories.

Adds a new duty for the board to develop and publish proxy voting guidelines treating climate change as a business and systemic risk, support shareholder resolutions reducing climate-change-contributing activity, and publicly justify in writing any decision not to support such resolutions.

Adds a new annual reporting requirement on the environmental sustainability of the board's investment decision-making process, including climate-related risk identification, financial impact assessment, and mitigation actions tied to federal climate-related reporting requirements.

Creates a new section directing the state auditor to conduct a biennial (starting December 1, 2027) evaluation of WSIB's climate-risk proxy voting guidelines and conformance, reporting findings and recommendations to the legislature.

whoAffected: No member class gains or loses benefits; the bill governs WSIB's investment and proxy-voting practices, indirectly affecting all beneficiaries of the pension funds and other public funds WSIB manages as fiduciary assets.
pointsOfInterest: This is not a benefits bill: it contains no multiplier, COLA, contribution, or eligibility change; it regulates WSIB's fiduciary investment and proxy-voting process, which is unusual for a bill classified as pension-related.

The bill layers a policy mandate (climate-risk-focused sustainability integration and proxy voting) onto WSIB's existing prudent-investor standard in RCW 43.33A.140, raising a potential tension between the statutory duty to maximize return at prudent risk and a directive to support climate-related shareholder resolutions, which analysts often flag as a fiduciary-duty overlay question even though the bill frames sustainability factors as return-maximizing.

The bill creates an external oversight mechanism (state auditor biennial review of proxy voting conformance, first due December 1, 2027) rather than legislature-facing SCPP oversight, a structurally different accountability channel than typical pension bills.

No fiscal note mechanics are present in the text itself (no appropriation language, no actuarial funding note, no contingent effective date, no emergency clause), consistent with a governance/process bill rather than a benefit-cost bill.

oneLine: HB 2471 adds a 0.5% per-year multiplier bonus for service beyond 30 years, prospectively, across the Plan 2 benefit formulas of TRS, SERS, and PERS.

provisions.detail: Adds a new bonus accrual of an additional 0.5% of average final compensation per year of service beyond 30 years, for TRS 2 members, applicable only to years of service earned after the section's effective date.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for TRS 3 members' defined benefit portion, prospective only.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for SERS 2 members, prospective only.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for SERS 3 members' defined benefit portion, prospective only.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for PERS 2 members, prospective only.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for PERS 3 members' defined benefit portion, prospective only.

whoAffected: Active PERS 2/3, SERS 2/3, and TRS 2/3 members who work beyond 30 years of service credit; no effect on members who separate at or before 30 years, and no retroactive effect on years already earned.
pointsOfInterest: The bonus applies only to years of service earned after the bill's effective date, so a member with 32 years at enactment gets the enhanced 2.5% rate only on future years beyond 30, not on the two years already worked past the 30-year mark; this creates a mixed-formula calculation for long-tenure members mid-career.

Benefit is narrowly targeted at a small population of very long-tenured members (30+ years of service), which in PERS/SERS/TRS Plan 2/3 is a relatively small share of the active membership, concentrating fiscal cost on a specific late-career cohort.

Uniform 0.5% bump is applied identically across six sections/three systems/two plan designs (Plan 2 and the DB half of Plan 3) rather than being tailored to each system's differing normal cost or funded status, suggesting a policy-driven rather than actuarially-calibrated design choice.

No emergency clause, no null-and-void-without-appropriation clause, and no contingent effective date appear in the bill text, meaning it would take effect under the standard 90-days-after-sine-die rule absent a fiscal note constraint added later; this leaves cost absorption to the standard PERS/SERS/TRS contribution rate-setting process rather than tying implementation to appropriated funding.

oneLine: ESSB 5294 replaces the open-ended minimum employer contribution rates for PERS/PSERS, SERS, and TRS Plan 1 unfunded liability with a declining rate schedule running through fiscal year 2027 (backstopped by a funding-contingent 0.50 percent floor thereafter), adds a state actuary review-and-recommend requirement, and cuts the fiscal year 2023 one-time general fund deposit to the TRS Plan 1 fund from $800 million to $250 million, effective immediately under an emergency clause.

provisions.detail: Caps the existing 3.50 percent minimum PERS/PSERS employer contribution rate for amortizing PERS Plan 1 unfunded actuarial accrued liability (UAAL) so it runs only through June 30, 2023, deleting the prior open-ended duration of 'until the actuarial value of assets ... equals 100 percent.'
Caps the existing 3.50 percent minimum SERS employer contribution rate for the same PERS Plan 1 UAAL so it runs only through August 31, 2023, removing the same open-ended 100 percent funded trigger.
Caps the existing 5.75 percent minimum TRS employer contribution rate for TRS Plan 1 UAAL so it runs only through August 31, 2023, removing the same open-ended trigger.

Establishes a new declining employer contribution rate schedule for PERS/PSERS (2.50%, 2.00%, 1.50%, 0.50% for fiscal years 2024-2027) dedicated to PERS Plan 1 UAAL, followed by a 0.50 percent minimum floor beginning July 1, 2027 that applies only while plan assets are below 100 percent of accrued liability.

Establishes the identical declining schedule (2.50% down to 0.50%, fiscal years 2024-2027) for SERS employer rates dedicated to PERS Plan 1 UAAL, followed by the same funding-contingent 0.50 percent floor beginning September 1, 2027.

Establishes a declining schedule for TRS employer rates dedicated to TRS Plan 1 UAAL running from 0.50 percent (FY2024-25) down to 0.00 percent (FY2026-27), followed by the same funding-contingent 0.50 percent floor beginning September 1, 2027.

Adds a new subsection directing the state actuary, upon completion of each biennial actuarial valuation, to review the minimum contribution rates and recommend adjustments to the Pension Funding Council for material changes in benefits, assumptions, methods, or experience, with any council changes subject to legislative revision.

Reduces the one-time fiscal year 2023 General Fund-State appropriation for deposit into the TRS Plan 1 fund (to be applied against the plan's unfunded actuarial accrued liability on June 30, 2023) from $800,000,000 to $250,000,000.
Declares an emergency for immediate preservation of public peace, health, safety, or state government operations, and sets the act's effective date as June 30, 2023.

whoAffected: Public employers in PERS/PSERS, SERS, and TRS (who pay the amortization-rate share of employer contributions) and the state general fund, not individual member benefits; PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 legacy funding levels are affected indirectly
pointsOfInterest: Section 2 cuts the FY2023 supplemental general-fund deposit into the TRS Plan 1 fund from $800 million to $250 million, a $550 million reduction in one-time UAAL paydown, timed to an effective date of June 30, 2023 (the last day of that fiscal year) under an emergency clause, meaning the reduced appropriation takes effect essentially concurrent with the close of the fiscal year it governs.

The bill swaps an indefinite 'minimum rate until 100 percent funded' floor for a fixed, declining stairstep schedule that sunsets in 2027, then reinstates a minimum rate only conditioned on funded status (below 100 percent) rather than a hard date - a shift from open-ended to time-boxed-plus-contingent design that could affect long-run amortization certainty.

The TRS schedule glides to a 0.00 percent employer rate by FY2026-2027 while the PERS/PSERS and SERS schedules bottom out at 0.50 percent, implying TRS Plan 1 is assumed to reach full funding on a faster track than PERS Plan 1 - worth checking against the underlying OSA valuation assumptions.

New subsection (7) creates a recurring state actuary review-and-recommend loop to the Pension Funding Council each biennial valuation, institutionalizing periodic rate reassessment rather than leaving the schedule static through 2027 as enacted.

oneLine: SB 5328 adds public safety telecommunicators (911 dispatchers) employed by PERS-covered employers to PSERS Plan 2 membership, gives existing PERS 2/3 telecommunicators a one-time election window to transfer prospectively as dual members, locks in PERS 1 telecommunicators, and makes new hires after June 1, 2024 automatic PSERS members.
whoAffected: Public safety telecommunicators (911 dispatchers/call-takers and their direct supervisors) employed by PERS-participating employers gain PSERS Plan 2 eligibility; PERS Plan 1 telecommunicators are excluded and remain in Plan 1; contract, nonprofit, and first-class-city telecommunicator employees are excluded entirely.

provisions.detail: Expands the RCW 41.37.010(12) definition of 'employer' to include any PERS-participating employer whose employees' primary responsibility is to receive, process, transmit, or dispatch 911 emergency and nonemergency calls, bringing those employers into PSERS coverage for that class of worker.

Adds a new RCW 41.37.010(19)(f) category to the definition of 'member,' extending PSERS eligibility to employees whose primary responsibility is to receive, process, transmit, or dispatch 911 emergency/nonemergency calls or to supervise such employees, plus a renumbered (g) for supervisors of newly eligible members.

Adds 'or psychological' to the legislative intent language in RCW 41.37.005 describing the physical risk that justifies separate PSERS treatment, textually extending the stated rationale for PSERS membership to psychological as well as physical occupational risk.

New section creates a one-time election period (January 1, 2024 through March 1, 2024) during which existing PERS Plan 2/3 telecommunicators employed as of June 1, 2024 may elect to become PSERS Plan 2 dual members under chapter 41.54 RCW, with membership effective prospectively from the election date and no transfer of accrued PERS service credit into PSERS.
provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.37 RCW (Sec. 4); ch. 41.54 RCW

provisions.detail: Telecommunicators who do not affirmatively elect to join PSERS by September 1, 2024 default to remaining in their current PERS plan, and PERS Plan 1 telecommunicators (members on or before June 1, 2019) are barred from switching and must remain in PERS Plan 1.
provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.37 RCW (Sec. 4)

provisions.detail: All newly hired telecommunicators meeting the eligibility definition who are hired on or after June 1, 2024 become PSERS members automatically, with no election required.
provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.37 RCW (Sec. 4)

pointsOfInterest: Section 1 is an unusual freestanding intent section that affirmatively narrows the bill's reach, explicitly disclaiming coverage for contract employees, nonprofit employees, and employees of first-class cities even though those entities may employ functionally identical telecommunicators; this creates a durable coverage gap that tracks employer type rather than job duties.

The election design (prospective-only join, no PERS service credit transfer into PSERS) avoids any actuarial cost of purchasing past service at PSERS rates, which limits the cost-shift to employers/plan compared to a full transfer-in design, but leaves electing members' PSERS benefit accrual starting from zero regardless of tenure.

The PERS Plan 1 carve-out (Sec. 4(5)) is a narrow, closed class: only those who were PERS 1 members on or before June 1, 2019 and remain PERS-covered telecommunicators past June 1, 2024. Because PERS 1 is closed and typically older/near-retirement, this avoids disrupting Plan 1's distinct benefit formula and funding status.

The 'or psychological' addition to the RCW 41.37.005 intent language is a small textual change but is notable because it is the only substantive amendment to the general PSERS rationale section, and could be read as legislative acknowledgment that psychological risk alone can justify PSERS-equivalent treatment for other occupational classes beyond telecommunicators.

oneLine: ESSB 5187, the 2023-25 operating budget (with 2021-23 second supplemental), makes one direct LEOFF 2 statutory change extending a narrow dual-contribution requirement, funds pension employer-contribution-rate increases and DRS costs contingent on separate companion bills, and cuts a prior TRS 1 unfunded-liability paydown from $800 million to $250 million.
whoAffected: LEOFF 2 officers/firefighters employed by port districts and higher-education institutions doing outside fee-for-service work; PERS 1 and TRS 1 retirees (contingent benefit-increase funding); WSPRS and LEOFF 2 members (contingent military-service-credit funding); TRS 1 plan funded status generally (reduced UAAL paydown)

provisions.detail: Extends into the 2023-2025 fiscal biennium the existing requirement that port districts and institutions of higher education pay both the employer and state pension contribution shares for LEOFF 2 members who are law enforcement officers or firefighters performing fee-for-service work for entities that are not their statutory 'employer'.

Funds a 0.12 percent increase in PERS, PSERS, and SERS employer contributions and a 0.23 percent increase in TRS employer contributions to pay for a one-time ongoing benefit increase for PERS 1 and TRS 1 retirees; the subsection is null and void, and the appropriations held in unallotted status, if Senate Bill No. 5350 is not enacted by June 30, 2023.

Funds a 0.13 percent increase in Washington state patrol retirement system employer contributions and a 0.01 percent increase in LEOFF 2 employer contributions to fund a military service credit purchase benefit; null and void if Senate Bill No. 5296 is not enacted by June 30, 2023.

Appropriates $181.3 million (biennium) in state contributions to LEOFF, made monthly per chapter 41.45 RCW, plus $12.3 million to the judicial retirement system and $600,000 to the judges' retirement system, made quarterly per chapters 2.10 and 2.12 RCW, and $18.704 million to the volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension fund.
provisions.cites: Sec. 727-728 (uncodified); ch. 41.45 RCW, ch. 2.10 RCW, ch. 2.12 RCW

provisions.detail: Amends a prior 2021-23 supplemental appropriation, reducing a lump-sum deposit into the teachers' retirement system plan 1 fund earmarked for paydown of the unfunded actuarial accrued liability from $800,000,000 to $250,000,000, with expenditure still directed for June 30, 2023.

Appropriates $34.491 million (2023-25) and $6.007 million (2021-23 supplemental) to the Department of Retirement Systems for 'pension system modernization,' subject to the IT-project oversight conditions of Sec. 701, plus smaller sums contingent on enactment of companion pension bills, including SB 5296 (military service credit, $143,000), SSB 5538 (postretirement nursing, $1,172,000), SB 5084 (self-insured pensions/fund, $41,000 plus $84,000/$84,000 from L&I accident and medical aid accounts), SB 5367 (inactive retirement accounts, $619,000), SB 5021 ($286,000), and ESSB 5399 (universal health care commission, $7,000); two supplemental items for SB 5676 (PERS/TRS 1 benefit increase, $48,000) and HB 1669 (PSERS disability benefits, $82,000) carry a June 30, 2022 enactment deadline that had already passed, so those amounts lapse.

pointsOfInterest: Sec. 1904 quietly cuts the TRS 1 UAAL supplemental paydown from $800 million to $250 million by amending a prior year's uncodified appropriation proviso rather than RCW, buried at the very end of the bill -- a $550 million swing in extra debt-reduction funding that materially affects TRS 1's funded-status trajectory and is easy to miss on a section-by-section RCW scan.

Nearly every pension item in this budget is a funding pass-through rather than a benefit change: contribution-rate bumps and DRS implementation costs for SB 5350, SB 5296, SB 5084, SB 5538, SB 5367, SB 5676, and HB 1669 are all null and void (appropriations unallotted) if those freestanding bills fail to pass -- the actual benefit design sits entirely outside this text.

The one direct LEOFF 2 statutory change (RCW 41.26.450) is a narrow anti-subsidy/cost-shifting mechanic, not a benefit change: it makes port districts and higher-ed institutions absorb both employer and state contribution shares when their LEOFF 2 officers or firefighters do outside fee-for-service work, preventing the state general fund from indirectly subsidizing third-party service arrangements.

The military-service-credit and PERS1/TRS1 benefit-increase funding is expressed as small employer contribution-rate increments (0.01%-0.23%) layered onto rates already set by the Pension Funding Council and the LEOFF 2 board and adjusted under SB 5294 (plan 1 UAAL rates), typical incremental normal-cost/UAAL funding mechanics rather than a rate-setting policy change in its own right.

oneLine: SB 5349 lifts the age-65 postretirement-employment bar for TRS 2/3, SERS 2/3, and PERS 2/3 members who retired under the 30-year/age-55 'alternate early retirement' option, letting them work up to 867 hours a year starting January 1, 2024, while consolidating and repealing a redundant narrower carve-out that previously served the same purpose.

provisions.detail: Removes, effective January 1, 2024, the prior rule barring alternate early retirees (30 service years, age 55, benefit reduced per statutory schedule) from any postretirement employment until age 65, and instead lets them work up to 867 hours per calendar year under the standard postretirement employment provisions before reaching 65; the pre-2024 bar remains in force through December 31, 2023.

Broadens the definition of 'employment with an employer' for these alternate early retirees before age 65 to include personal service contracts and service as a temporary or project employee, then narrows it after age 65 to only the statutory 'employer' definition, changing what counts against the hours cap depending on the retiree's age.

Repeals a narrower, now-redundant subsection that had separately authorized up to 867 hours of postretirement work without benefit suspension for alternate early retirees who reentered nonadministrative employment after June 9, 2016, since the same 867-hour allowance is now granted directly in the eligibility sections; remaining subsections are relettered accordingly.

whoAffected: TRS 2/3, SERS 2/3, and PERS 2/3 members who retired (or will retire) under the 30-service-year/age-55 'alternate early retirement' option, a narrower subset of the general early-retiree population
pointsOfInterest: The bill's substantive reach is confined to one narrow retiree subclass, alternate early retirees who elected the 30-year/age-55 reduced-benefit path, even though it amends nine sections across three systems' plan 2/3 structures.

It liberalizes postretirement work rules by removing an age-65 employment bar that had specifically targeted this subclass, raising the usual return-to-work/benefit-suspension policy tension (workforce retention and staffing shortages, particularly in schools, versus double-dipping and cost-shifting concerns) without any accompanying fiscal note or study language in the bill text itself.

The employment definition is widened (capturing personal service contracts and temp/project work) for retirees under 65 but narrowed for retirees over 65 in the same sentence, an asymmetric anti-loophole drafting choice whose practical effect is muted by the fact that the underlying hours-limit prohibition it guards is being lifted at the same time.

The repealed carve-out in the reemployment sections overlapped with still-active, separately sunsetting (July 1, 2025) COVID-era school-district reemployment relief enacted by 2022 c 110, so this bill is layered on top of an already temporary, staggered set of postretirement employment rules rather than a clean baseline.

oneLine: SB 5350 grants a one-time 3 percent COLA, capped at $110 a month, to PERS 1 and TRS 1 retirees on the rolls as of July 1, 2022, excludes certain survivor and disability beneficiaries from that increase, and directs the Select Committee on Pension Policy to study an ongoing COLA tied to paydown of the plans' unfunded liability, effective immediately under an emergency clause.

provisions.detail: Adds a fourth-tier one-time benefit increase for TRS Plan 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2022, effective July 1, 2023: 3 percent of the monthly benefit, capped at $110.00.

Adds a matching fourth-tier one-time benefit increase for PERS Plan 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2022, effective July 1, 2023: 3 percent of the monthly benefit, capped at $110.00.
Excludes TRS 1 beneficiaries receiving benefits under the survivor/disability provisions of RCW 41.32.489 or 41.32.540 from the increase in this section.
Excludes PERS 1 beneficiaries receiving benefits under RCW 41.40.1984 from the increase in this section.
Restates the prior three tiers' dollar caps in numeral form ($62.50, $62.50, $110.00) rather than spelled-out text, a non-substantive drafting cleanup.
Uncodified legislative finding states that an ongoing COLA for PERS 1/TRS 1 beneficiaries may not be affordable until required employer UAAL contribution rates are reduced or eliminated.

Directs SCPP, during the 2023-2025 fiscal biennium, to study and recommend an ongoing COLA for PERS 1/TRS 1 beneficiaries, with any recommendation to consider employer contribution rate stability and to coordinate the COLA's effective date with reduction or elimination of the unfunded actuarial accrued liability.

whoAffected: PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 retirees/beneficiaries on the benefit rolls as of July 1, 2022, excluding those drawing survivor or disability benefits under RCW 41.32.489, 41.32.540, or 41.40.1984
pointsOfInterest: This is the fourth successive one-time, capped-dollar COLA layered onto the same two statutes (2018, 2020, 2022, now 2023) rather than a permanent indexed COLA; the ad hoc pattern itself is the policy, not a one-off fix.

Section 2 explicitly conditions any future ongoing COLA on reduction or elimination of the UAAL, an unusual instance of the legislature pre-committing a benefit study's scope to employer cost sequencing rather than beneficiary need.

The survivor/disability carve-outs under RCW 41.32.489/41.32.540 and 41.40.1984 have been excluded from every iteration of this ad hoc COLA since 2018; the bill perpetuates rather than revisits that exclusion, worth flagging for equity review.

An emergency clause is used for what is functionally a routine, incremental benefit bump rather than a genuine peace/health/safety measure; its practical effect is to move the effective date up and to place the act beyond referendum.

oneLine: ESSB 5424 authorizes law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible/part-time work policies and, via a dual-track technical amendment sequenced against a companion tribal-officer provision, extends LEOFF Plan 2 membership and statewide peace-officer status to less-than-full-time commissioned officers beginning July 1, 2024.

provisions.detail: Adds a new section to chapter 49.28 RCW authorizing general and limited authority Washington law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible work policies (part-time work, alternative shifts), with guardrails barring displacement of full-time officers and preserving collective bargaining obligations and existing bargaining units.

Reenacts and amends the chapter 10.93 RCW definitions of "general authority Washington peace officer" and "limited authority Washington peace officer" by striking the existing "full-time" qualifier, so part-time commissioned officers now qualify as peace officers under that chapter.

Amends the currently effective version of the LEOFF definitions section to add a new law enforcement officer category, effective July 1, 2024, covering commissioned, fully compensated officers working less than full time who otherwise meet the existing qualifications, making them LEOFF Plan 2 members.

Makes the identical part-time officer eligibility addition to the version of RCW 41.26.030 that takes effect July 1, 2025 (as already amended by 2023 c 77 to add a tribal police department officer category), inserting it as a new subsection so both changes coexist.

Section 3 (the July 2024 version of the amendment) expires July 1, 2025, and Section 4 (the tribal-officer-compatible version) takes effect July 1, 2025, sequencing the two amendments to the same subsection so there is no gap or conflict in coverage.

whoAffected: Part-time (less-than-full-time), fully compensated general and limited authority Washington peace officers and law enforcement officers, who newly qualify for peace-officer status statewide and for LEOFF Plan 2 membership; full-time officers and existing bargaining units are protected from displacement.
pointsOfInterest: Uses a dual-track (expire/effective) amendment pair on the same RCW 41.26.030 subsection to sequence this change against the already-enacted 2023 c 77 tribal-officer provision, a standard but easy-to-miss WA drafting mechanic that can obscure which version of the definition is live at a given date.

Pure eligibility/definitional expansion: no change to contribution rates, benefit multiplier, COLA, vesting, or funding policy; cost impact depends entirely on how many employers voluntarily adopt flexible work policies under the new chapter 49.28 section, since adoption is permissive ("may"), not mandatory.

Existing LEOFF service-credit thresholds (90/70-hour full, half, and quarter service-credit months) already accommodate part-time work, so no new crediting mechanism was needed, but final average salary for Plan 2 is based on the highest 60 consecutive service-credit months, meaning a late-career shift to part-time schedule would generally lower, not spike, a member's benefit.

The RCW 10.93.020 change reaches beyond LEOFF and pension eligibility into the general peace-officer certification and mutual-aid framework, conferring statewide peace-officer authority on part-time officers, not just retirement-system membership.

oneLine: SB 5468 amends the LEOFF definitions statute, RCW 41.26.030, to add promotional (non-civil-service-tested) full-time firefighter positions requiring firefighting experience to the definition of 'firefighter,' keeping members who are promoted within a fire department in LEOFF rather than losing that status, and separately fixes a stale internal citation.

provisions.detail: Adds new RCW 41.26.030(17)(d), defining 'firefighter' to include any person serving full time, fully compensated, as an employee of a fire department in a position that requires an experienced firefighter, so that a firefighter promoted into such a position keeps LEOFF membership instead of falling outside the statutory definition.

Relabels existing subsections (17)(d) through (h) as (e) through (i) to accommodate the new (d), including the carve-out for executive secretaries of fire protection district associations, which continues to state it does not apply to plan 2 members.
Corrects an internal cross-reference from RCW 18.73.030(12) to RCW 18.73.030(13) in the EMT-firefighter clause, conforming to a 2022 renumbering of that statute noted by the code reviser.

whoAffected: Firefighters promoted into full-time positions within a fire department that require firefighting experience (e.g., fire marshal, training officer, inspector roles) but lack a distinct civil service firefighter exam, who gain continued/clarified LEOFF membership rather than risking exclusion from the definition of 'firefighter.'
pointsOfInterest: The new (17)(d) standard - 'a position that requires an experienced firefighter' - is undefined and less concrete than the criteria used elsewhere in the same definition (civil service exam, named dispatcher/EMT certification requirements), leaving the employer or DRS to determine case by case which promotional positions qualify.

Unlike the neighboring carve-outs in (17)(e) and (17)(f), which expressly state they do not apply to plan 2 members, the new (17)(d) contains no such limitation, so on its face it extends to both plan 1 and plan 2, which broadens the fiscal exposure beyond a plan 1-only fix.

Because LEOFF is a closed, more generous system relative to PERS for local government employees, retaining promoted firefighters in LEOFF rather than letting them default into PERS has an actuarial cost and would ordinarily warrant a fiscal note from the state actuary given the membership-eligibility expansion.

The bill piggybacks an unrelated technical citation fix (18.73.030 renumbering) onto the same amendatory section as the substantive membership change, which is common drafting practice in RCW 41.26.030 but obscures the size of the substantive change within a large omnibus definitions section.

oneLine: SSB 5538 creates a temporary, sunsetting (through July 1, 2026) return-to-work carve-out in both PSERS and PERS letting retired licensed nurses working nonadministrative positions for a state agency draw full pension payments while working up to 1,040 hours a year, bypassing the usual 867-hour postretirement work cap, and takes effect immediately under an emergency clause.

provisions.detail: Adds new subsection (2)(b) to RCW 41.37.050 (PSERS) letting a retiree who has met the break-in-employment requirement and who takes a nonadministrative licensed-nurse position with a state agency keep receiving pension payments while working, until service exceeds 1,040 hours in a calendar year, effective from the act's effective date through July 1, 2026.

Adds new subsection (2)(c) to RCW 41.40.037 (PERS, plans 1/2/3, including alternate early retirees under RCW 41.40.630(3)(b) and 41.40.820(3)(b)) granting the identical nonadministrative licensed-nurse, state-agency, 1,040-hour, effective-date-to-July 1, 2026 carve-out from pension suspension.
New uncodified Section 3 declares the act necessary for immediate preservation of public peace, health, or safety and gives it an immediate effective date.

whoAffected: Retired PSERS and PERS members (plans 1, 2, and 3, including alternate early retirees) who return to nonadministrative licensed-nursing positions with a state agency gain a temporary, higher (1,040-hour) postretirement work threshold before pension suspension; other retirees remain capped at 867 hours.
pointsOfInterest: The carve-out is drawn extremely narrowly: nonadministrative, licensed-nurse, state-agency positions only, mirroring but distinct from the existing school-district nonadministrative-position carve-out already in RCW 41.40.037(2)(b) (which runs through July 1, 2025) — this bill effectively extends the same double-dipping relief mechanism to a new, unnamed 'state agency' population, almost certainly targeting DOC or DSHS institutional nursing shortages.

Raises the postretirement work ceiling from 867 hours (the standard limit in both sections' (2)(a)) to 1,040 hours for this class, a nontrivial expansion of allowable hours worked while drawing full pension, which increases double-dipping cost exposure to the retirement systems for the duration of the carve-out.

The sunset date (July 1, 2026) is set well past the bill's own emergency immediate-effective-date, giving roughly three years of carve-out life — long for what is framed as a stopgap staffing fix, and worth checking against any fiscal note for projected cost.

Emergency clause plus immediate effective date for what is otherwise a narrow personnel-policy tweak signals urgent, likely institution-specific staffing pressure (e.g., 24-hour nursing coverage at a state facility) rather than a broad systemic pension change.

oneLine: SB 5625 creates a DRS retiree ombuds office funded by system expense-fund/HCA fees, tolls and lengthens member appeal deadlines with retroactive reopening of dismissed claims, expands LEOFF 2 disability-review rights and the 'basic salary' definition used for benefits, and excludes DRS administrative/UAL fees from the cost of purchasing service credit.

provisions.detail: Creates a governor-appointed office of the ombuds for retiree benefits within DRS, with a six-year term, removal only for cause, staffing capped at four for the first two years, defined qualifications, advocacy/complaint-resolution/referral duties, a toll-free line, confidentiality of records, good-faith immunity, whistleblower protection for DRS employees who cooperate, a dedicated assistant attorney general, and a required website link.
provisions.cites: new sections added to chapter 41.50 RCW (Secs. 1-9, 12, 19)

provisions.detail: Funds the ombuds office through the DRS expense fund (RCW 41.50.110) and the health care authority administrative account (RCW 41.05.130), i.e., through system/employer rate charges rather than a general fund appropriation.

Requires an annual ombuds report to the governor, the Select Committee on Pension Policy, and the LEOFF 2 board, describing issues handled, monitoring activity, and recommended remedial action, first due April 1, 2024.
Tolls a member's or retiree's time to file a notice of appeal under chapter 34.05 RCW while a matter is under ombuds investigation, until the ombuds decides and DRS responds.

Defines 'in the line of duty' for LEOFF/PSERS purposes to match 'in the course of employment' under the industrial insurance title, makes LEOFF 2 disability-retirement denials issued before the effective date subject to department review for line-of-duty status, and requires an occupational assessment whenever a disability denial rests on capacity for employment.
provisions.cites: new section (Sec. 14); chapter 41.26 RCW; chapter 41.37 RCW; Title 51 RCW

provisions.detail: Amends the DRS expense-fund statute to exclude the department's administrative fee and any employer unfunded-liability charge from the calculation of employer contributions charged to a member when purchasing service credit.

Sets a minimum 90-day notice-of-appeal deadline for DRS decisions, requires at least a 90-day toll when DRS requests supporting information, and allows refiling of any claim previously dismissed for untimely appeal after such an information request.

Treats survivor-election change requests made between June 11, 2020 and the date IRS approval is received as timely, with any resulting benefit change effective only prospectively upon federal approval.

Expands the LEOFF plan 2 'basic salary' definition to include holiday payments (in addition to overtime already counted) and sick or vacation leave used by the member, increasing the compensation base used to calculate final average salary and benefits; also corrects a cross-reference to RCW 18.73.030's renumbered subsection.

whoAffected: DRS-administered system retirees and members generally gain an ombuds/appeal-rights channel; LEOFF plan 2 members and disability applicants (including those previously denied) gain expanded compensation counting and a retroactive disability-review right; PERS plan 1 members with pre-1998 survivor elections and post-2020 election-change requesters gain a curative timeliness fix; employers bear the ombuds funding cost through DRS expense-fund and HCA account charges.
pointsOfInterest: Creates a standing governance body (the ombuds office) with confidentiality, immunity, and subpoena-adjacent investigatory features, funded entirely through system expense-fund and HCA administrative-account rate charges rather than a general fund appropriation - a durable cost embedded in employer billing rates rather than a one-time budget item.

Section 14 reopens LEOFF 2 disability denials issued before the bill's effective date for line-of-duty redetermination, and Section 16 lets previously dismissed appeals be refiled - both create open-ended retroactive liability and reprocessing exposure with no cost estimate or funding offset stated in the bill text itself.

Section 18's expansion of LEOFF 2 'basic salary' to include holiday pay and used sick/vacation leave raises the compensation base used for final average salary, a modest but real spiking-adjacent cost shift onto the plan since it increases benefit levels without an offsetting contribution-rate change in the bill.

Section 15 shifts a cost away from members purchasing service credit (excluding DRS admin fee and employer UAL charge from the purchase price) - a narrow but precedent-setting exclusion that could invite requests to exclude other administrative surcharges elsewhere in the DRS fee structure.

oneLine: SB 5881 amends RCW 41.40.023 to add a new PERS membership exclusion for part-time bus drivers serving naval shipyards for a public transportation benefit area who are hired on or after the effective date and simultaneously work full-time for the federal government under FERS.

provisions.detail: Adds new subsection (23) excluding from PERS membership persons hired on or after the effective date who are employed by a public transportation benefit area (per RCW 36.57A.010) as part-time bus drivers serving naval shipyards, if simultaneously employed full-time by the federal government and contributing to the federal employees' retirement system.

Splits the strike-through reference to the 'volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund' into two separately named funds (the firefighters' fund and the reserve officers' fund) to conform subsection (4)(c) to a 2023 statutory fund split.
provisions.cites: RCW 41.40.023(4)(c); conforms to 2023 c 73 s 6 amending RCW 41.24.030

provisions.detail: Updates the reference to the liquor control board to the liquor and cannabis board in subsection (10), a technical rename already reflected in 2015 c 70 s 3.
Replaces the trailing conjunction after subsection (21) and adds 'and' after subsection (22) to grammatically accommodate the new subsection (23).

whoAffected: A narrow class of newly hired part-time transit bus drivers who serve naval shipyard routes for a public transportation benefit area while also working full-time federal jobs under FERS; they are excluded from PERS membership, while current employees in that role before the effective date are unaffected.
pointsOfInterest: The carve-out is defined by an unusually specific fact pattern (part-time PTBA bus driver, naval shipyard routes, simultaneous full-time federal employment under FERS) rather than by job classification alone, suggesting it targets a known, small, identifiable group of workers (likely near a specific shipyard such as PSNS in Bremerton) rather than a general policy class.

The exclusion is prospective only ('hired on or after the effective date'), so it avoids disrupting existing members' accrued PERS service, but it also means current dual-employed drivers keep dual coverage indefinitely while new hires cannot, creating a two-tier workforce doing the same job.

The policy rationale mirrors the existing portability logic in the 1999 c 286 intent note appended to this same RCW section (avoiding low-value PERS membership for workers whose real retirement value lies in a more portable federal system), extending that reasoning from elected or mobile officials to a specific transit labor pool.

The bill piggybacks two unrelated technical reviser-note corrections (the 2023 volunteer firefighters'/reserve officers' fund split and the liquor-to-cannabis board rename) onto the same section being reopened for the substantive change, a common but easy-to-miss pattern when scanning for the bill's actual policy content.

oneLine: SB 6000 replaces the "period of war" test with a campaign, expeditionary, or service medal/badge test for no-cost interruptive military service credit across LEOFF 2, PERS, PSERS, SERS, TRS, and WSPRS, and applies the expanded eligibility retroactively, requiring DRS to recalculate benefits and contributions for members who already retired.

provisions.detail: Replaces the requirement that interruptive military service occur "during a period of war as defined in RCW 41.04.005" with a requirement that the member was awarded a campaign, expeditionary, or service badge or medal, as the alternate (no member-contribution) path to up to five years of free service credit for the member, for a deceased member's survivors, and for a disabled member.

Same substitution of the medal/badge criterion for the period-of-war criterion governing no-cost interruptive military service credit for the member, surviving spouse/child, and totally incapacitated member.

Same substitution of the medal/badge criterion for the period-of-war criterion governing no-cost interruptive military service credit for the member, surviving spouse/child, and totally incapacitated member.

Same substitution of the medal/badge criterion for the period-of-war criterion governing no-cost interruptive military service credit for the member, surviving spouse/child, and totally incapacitated member.

Same substitution of the medal/badge criterion for the period-of-war criterion governing no-cost interruptive military service credit for the member, surviving spouse/child, and totally incapacitated member.

Same substitution of the medal/badge criterion for the period-of-war criterion governing no-cost interruptive military service credit, applied to the WSPRS provisions for members commissioned on or after January 1, 2003, their survivors, and disabled members; leaves intact the separate pre-2003-commission provision allowing up to five years of credited uniformed service without regard to whether the member left Patrol employment to serve.

New uncodified section makes the expanded no-cost military service credit eligibility retroactive for all RCW 41.50.030 retirement systems and requires the department to recalculate retirement benefits and adjust contributions for members who retired before the act's effective date if they have eligible military service.

whoAffected: Members of LEOFF 2, PERS 2/3, PSERS 2, SERS 2/3, TRS 2/3, and WSPRS (post-2003-commission) who performed interruptive military service and hold a campaign, expeditionary, or service medal but did not serve during a formally defined "period of war" gain no-cost service credit eligibility, as do their surviving spouses/domestic partners/children and members who became totally incapacitated during such service; already-retired members with qualifying service gain retroactive benefit recalculation.
pointsOfInterest: Section 7 requires DRS to retroactively recalculate benefits and adjust contributions for members who already retired, an unusual and administratively heavy remedy for a pension bill that implies the department must identify and reprocess an unknown population of past retirements.

Swapping the "period of war" test (tied to statutorily enumerated war periods under RCW 41.04.005) for a medal/badge test is more easily documented via DD-214 but likely expands the eligible population to campaigns and operations never designated a "period of war" (e.g., certain peacetime deployments and campaign medals), broadening the no-cost credit pool without a corresponding member contribution.

Because the credit is "no-cost" to the member once medal/badge proof is furnished, the fiscal exposure lands on the employer and state contribution side (the department bills the employer/state under each system's funding statutes), so the eligibility expansion is a cost shift to employers/the state rather than a member-funded benefit.

The amendment is executed nearly word-for-word across six separate chapters/systems (LEOFF 2, TRS, SERS, PSERS, PERS, WSPRS), which is efficient drafting but means any actuarial or drafting error in the template propagates across all six systems simultaneously; the WSPRS section also preserves a distinct, older, narrower carve-out for members commissioned before January 1, 2003.

oneLine: SSB 5871 replaces Washington's honorable-discharge standard with a broader "qualifying discharge" definition across roughly 30 veteran-benefit statutes (tuition, hiring credit, licensing, bar admission, veterans' home admission, tax exemptions), but leaves the PERS and legacy firefighters'/police pension military-service-credit-purchase statutes on the old honorable-discharge/period-of-war standard.

provisions.detail: Redefines "veteran" for purposes of RCW 41.16.220, 41.20.050, and 41.40.170 by replacing the honorable-discharge requirement with the new "qualifying discharge" standard.
Redefines the general-purpose "veteran" status (used for hiring credit, tuition, licensing, and dozens of other statutes) to substitute "qualifying discharge" for "honorable discharge."

Creates a new statewide "qualifying discharge" standard covering honorable, general-under-honorable, and other-than-honorable discharges tied to VA benefit eligibility, plus any discharge characterization resulting from sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression.
Directs the department of veterans affairs to run an outreach program explaining the act's eligibility changes, beginning on the section's effective date.
Ties WWII-era veteran bar-admission eligibility to the RCW 41.04.007 veteran definition instead of an honorable/other-than-dishonorable service standard.
Repeals the disability-discharge bar-admission provision, superseded by the new qualifying-discharge standard.
Extends the post-discharge gambling-license renewal grace period to any qualifying discharge rather than only an honorable discharge.
Allows discretionary high school diplomas for wartime-service veterans using the qualifying-discharge standard instead of "honorably discharged member."

Substitutes qualifying discharge for honorable service in the 10-year-service resident-tuition classification, cross-references the new LGBTQ-discharge carve-out, and explicitly excludes bad conduct discharge and officer dismissal (along with dishonorable discharge) from residency eligibility.
Redefines "eligible veteran or national guard member" for tuition waivers and textbook stipends using the qualifying-discharge standard.
Applies the qualifying-discharge standard to the teacher conditional-scholarship/loan-repayment program's veteran definition.
Ties the veterans' hiring and promotional examination scoring credit to qualifying discharge rather than honorable discharge.

Substitutes qualifying discharge for the prior honorable/not-undesirable-bad-conduct-dishonorable test in the state civil service veterans' layoff-and-seniority credit rule (up to five years added to unbroken state service).
Extends the fire and police civil-service commissions' entrance-examination military credit (keyed to RCW 41.04.010) to any qualifying discharge.

Clarifies that firefighters' relief-and-pension credit for wartime military service (up to five years, purchased by member contribution) requires an honorably discharged veteran or an honorable physical-reasons discharge, and explicit service "during a period of war" -- retaining the pre-bill honorable-discharge standard rather than the act's new qualifying-discharge definition.

Applies the same honorable-discharge-plus-period-of-war standard (not the new qualifying-discharge definition) to police relief-and-pension credit for wartime military service, purchasable up to five years by member contribution.

Adds an explicit "period of war" requirement (RCW 41.04.005) to PERS military-leave service-credit purchases, extends eligibility to honorable physical-reasons discharges, and corrects an erroneous cross-reference from RCW 41.40.005 to RCW 41.04.005 governing service credit for members who become retirement-eligible while still serving; survivor and total-incapacitation service-credit provisions continue to require proof of honorable service/discharge and are not updated to the new qualifying-discharge standard.
Extends the professional-license moratorium and post-discharge renewal grace period (director of licensing, and secretary of health) to any qualifying discharge.
Ties the certified veteran-owned business ownership test to the RCW 41.04.007 veteran definition rather than a separately-stated honorable/medical-honorable standard.

Redefines armed forces, Pearl Harbor, Purple Heart, and veterans/military emblem license-plate eligibility, and driver's-license veteran designation, around the qualifying-discharge standard, with the license-plate provisions delayed to an April 1, 2025 effective date and the current armed-forces-plate section expiring the same date.

Broadens state veterans' home admission from "honorably discharged" veterans of the armed forces to veterans meeting RCW 41.04.007's discharge requirements or otherwise eligible for VA medical care, and widens the covered branch definition from "armed forces" to "uniformed services."
Repeals an obsolete 1919/1923 statute recording honorable discharges for Spanish-American War and World War I veterans.
Substitutes qualifying discharge for honorable discharge across the county veterans'-assistance-fund veteran definition's several subcategories.

Changes the veteran-employment campaign's "veteran" definition from "honorably discharged" to the RCW 41.04.007 definition, and similarly updates reduced-rate hunting/fishing license eligibility for disabled veterans.

Removes the requirement that a deceased veteran's DD-214 show "honorable conditions" for a surviving spouse's property-tax exemption claim, substituting proof of qualification under RCW 41.04.005 with added documentation paths for other-than-honorable decedents, and exempts the act from standard tax-preference automatic-expiration/JLARC review requirements.

whoAffected: Washington veterans with other-than-honorable or general discharges -- particularly those discharged due to sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression, or otherwise eligible for VA monetary benefits -- gain broad state veteran-benefit eligibility, except that PERS and the legacy firefighters'/police pension military-service-credit-purchase statutes (RCW 41.16.220, 41.20.050, 41.40.170) retain the pre-bill honorable-discharge/period-of-war standard and are not extended to this newly eligible population.
pointsOfInterest: The bill's stated purpose is to align state veteran benefits with federal VA eligibility and to remedy discriminatory discharges, but the three military-service-credit-purchase pension statutes (RCW 41.16.220 firefighters, RCW 41.20.050 police, RCW 41.40.170 PERS) are conspicuously not updated to the new "qualifying discharge" definition -- they keep "honorably discharged" (plus a narrow physical-discharge exception) and, for PERS, add an explicit "period of war" test. LGBTQ-discharged and OTH veterans become eligible for tuition, hiring credit, license renewal, and bar admission under the new standard, but not for purchasing military service credit in these three retirement systems.

Section 20(4)(b) fixes a longstanding scrivener's-type cross-reference error (RCW 41.40.005 corrected to RCW 41.04.005) in the PERS military-service-credit statute -- a pure technical correction bundled into an otherwise substantive bill.

Service-credit purchase under the three pension statutes remains member-funded (restoration of withdrawn contributions or payment of the contribution rate for the credited period), so there is no direct employer or state cost-shift from this bill; the effect is instead a mismatch between who counts as a "veteran" for general benefit administration and who can buy military service credit toward a pension.

The only hard contingent effective date in the bill (Secs. 37-38) applies to license-plate provisions, which take effect and cause the prior armed-forces-plate section to expire on the same date, April 1, 2025 -- creating a brief window where DOL's plate-eligibility standard lags every other agency's qualifying-discharge standard under the act.
